sublevels.description: Pharmacodynamics (PD) is an area of pharmacology concerned with the relationship between a drug’s concentration at the site of action and the resulting effect, as well as the measurement of that relationship within an individual or group. Factors influencing a drug’s pharmacodynamics include the concentration of the drug target and the signalling pathways downstream.

sublevels.name: Pharmacokinetics
sublevels.description: Pharmacokinetics is an area of pharmacology concerned with the time course of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (collectively ADME) of drugs from biological systems in order to understand the effect of the drug, or of the organism, on the drug's impact. Pharmacokinetic parameters can also include toxicology and a drug’s liberation from its medicinal formulation.

sublevels.name: Receptor Pharmacology
sublevels.description: Receptor pharmacology is the study of the interactions of receptors with drugs/pharmaceuticals and other xenobiotics. A basic tenet of receptor pharmacology is that a drug’s effect is directly proportional to the number of occupied receptors. Also, the duration of the drug effect is related to the association and dissociation rates of the drug–receptor complex.

sublevels.name: Epidemiology
sublevels.description: Epidemiology is a field of medicine that studies the incidence, causes and effects of diseases in populations, and patterns within these. It has a key role in protecting public health and can provide valuable information for developing new medicines, such as revealing risk factors for a particular disease.

sublevels.name: Preclinical Research
sublevels.description: Preclinical research involves the evaluation of potential therapeutic interventions in cells and animals. Candidates for entry into clinical trials can then be selected based on their effectiveness and safety in disease models. All drugs require data from various toxicological preclinical studies to support their potential safety in humans before clinical trials can begin.

sublevels.name: Experimental Models of Disease
sublevels.description: Experimental models of disease are used to investigate processes thought to be involved in human diseases, and to evaluate and select drug candidates that affect these processes to support their progression into clinical trials. They typically involve animals in which processes that are considered to be sufficiently similar to those in human disease are either induced or naturally occur.

sublevels.name: Medical Microbiology
sublevels.description: Pathological processes in the human body caused by viruses, bacteria and parasites.

sublevels.name: Veterinary Microbiology
sublevels.description: Veterinary Microbiology is the study of the agents responsible for causing animal infections: bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites.

sublevels.name: Infectious-Disease Diagnostics
sublevels.description: Infectious-disease diagnostics is the procedure by which the causative agent of an infectious disease is identified and often characterized. It can be based solely on clinical presentation or more rigorous diagnostic tests, such as culturing of the infectious agent, microscopy, biochemical screens and molecular methods.

sublevels.name: Infectious-Disease Epidemiology
sublevels.description: The study of the incidence and spread of infectious diseases in populations over time. Host, pathogen and environmental factors are monitored to determine the dynamics of infection, the ultimate goal of which is to devise intervention strategies. Molecular methods, such as phylogenomics, can be used to accurately track pathogens.

sublevels.name: Pathogens
sublevels.description: Pathogens are infectious agents, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or parasite, that cause disease when they colonize a host organism.

sublevels.name: Infectious Diseases
sublevels.description: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogenic microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, parasites or fungi, that infect a host organism and can be spread, directly or indirectly, from one organism to another. An infectiologist manages nosocomial (healthcare-acquired) or community-acquired infections.

sublevels.name: Antimicrobials
sublevels.description: Antibiotics are substances that inhibit the growth of microbes such as bacteria, microscopic fungi or protozoans.

sublevels.name: Toxicology
sublevels.description: Toxicology is a scientific discipline, overlapping with biology, chemistry, pharmacology, and medicine, that involves the study of the adverse effects of chemical substances on living organisms and the practice of diagnosing and treating exposures to toxins and toxicants.

sublevels.name: Medical Biochemistry
sublevels.description: Medical Biochemistry is the application of biochemical principles to the understanding, diagnosis, and treatment of human diseases. It focuses on the biochemical basis of pathology, clinical biomarkers, metabolic disorders, molecular diagnostics, and therapeutic interventions relevant to human health. The field supports clinical decision‑making through biochemical diagnostics, laboratory testing, and the interpretation of molecular and metabolic abnormalities in patients.

sublevels.name: Translational Research
sublevels.description: Translational research involves the application of knowledge gained through basic research to studies that could support the development of new products. For example, translational research in the field of medicine may involve using knowledge of the biology of a disease to identify and evaluate chemical compounds in disease models, with a view to selecting potential candidate drugs to advance into clinical trials.

sublevels.name: Biomarkers
sublevels.description: A biomarker is a biological characteristic that is objectively measured and evaluated as an indicator of normal biological or pathological processes, or a response to a therapeutic intervention. Examples include patterns of gene expression, levels of a particular protein in body fluids, or changes in electrical activity in the brain.

sublevels.name: Prognostic Markers
sublevels.description: Prognostic markers are biological characteristics that are objectively measured and evaluated to predict the course of a disease or a response to a therapeutic intervention among patients with the same characteristic. Examples include the presence of a particular gene variant, patterns of gene expression or levels of a particular protein in body fluids.

sublevels.name: Predictive Markers
sublevels.description: Predictive markers indicate the likely response to a specific therapy, identifying whether a patient is expected to benefit from, be resistant to, or be harmed by a particular treatment.

sublevels.name: Diagnostic Markers
sublevels.description: Diagnostic markers are biological parameters that aid the diagnosis of diseases. Examples include the presence of particular genetic variants and the levels of particular proteins in body fluids.

sublevels.name: Surgery
sublevels.description: Surgery is a procedure in which incision and physical manipulation are used to treat a patient with an injury or a disease. The patient's tissues are cut during this technique to permit the manipulation of tissues that are otherwise inaccessible.

sublevels.name: Transplantation
sublevels.description: Transplantation is the procedure of transferring a tissue or organ from one individual to another or from one site to another within a single individual. The transplanted tissue or organ replaces damaged or absent tissue, and is functional in the recipient.

sublevels.name: Organ Transplantation
sublevels.description: Organ transplantation is a procedure in which a functional, intact organ is transferred from one individual to another. The organ is then functional in the recipient. This type of transplantation can occur between individuals of the same species or between individuals of different species.

sublevels.name: Transplantation Tolerance
sublevels.description: Transplantation tolerance is a state in which the immune system of the recipient of a tissue or organ transplantation does not attack the transplanted tissue. Transplantation tolerance is induced by immunosuppression, and prevents rejection of the transplant.

sublevels.name: Autologous Transplantation
sublevels.description: Autologous transplantation is a procedure in which an individual's own tissue is used to replace their damaged tissue. The removed tissue can be used immediately at a different site. Alternatively, the tissue can be removed, the individual or the tissue can be treated, and the tissue can then be replaced, for example cell transplantation.

sublevels.name: Cell Transplantation
sublevels.description: Cell transplantation is a procedure in which cells, often stem cells or cells that can be induced to become pluripotent stem cells, are transferred to a site where the tissue is damaged or diseased. The transfer can occur within an individual (autologous transplantation), between individuals, or between species. Cells can be treated before implantation.

sublevels.name: Minimally Invasive Surgery
sublevels.description: Minimally invasive procedures (also known as minimally invasive surgeries) encompass surgical techniques that limit the size of incisions needed, thereby reducing wound healing time, associated pain, and risk of infection.

sublevels.name: Neurosurgery
sublevels.description: Neurosurgery is a surgical procedure that uses invasive techniques to diagnose, investigate and/or treat a neurological disorder, disease or injury. For example, to remove a brain tumour or insert a deep brain stimulation device.

sublevels.name: Pediatric Surgery
sublevels.description: Pediatric surgery is a subspecialty of surgery involving the surgery of fetuses, infants, children, adolescents, and young adults.

sublevels.name: Vascular Surgery
sublevels.description: Vascular surgery refers to open surgeries and minimally-invasive procedures that treat a range of blood vessel problems. These include aortic aneurysms, peripheral artery disease, carotid artery disease and chronic venous insufficiency.

sublevels.name: General Surgery
sublevels.description: General surgery is a surgical specialty that focuses on alimentary canal and abdominal contents including the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, appendix and bile ducts, and often the thyroid gland. They also deal with diseases involving the skin, breast, soft tissue, trauma, peripheral artery disease and hernias and perform endoscopic as such as gastroscopy, colonoscopy and laparoscopic procedures.

sublevels.name: Bariatric Surgery
sublevels.description: Bariatric surgery is a type of surgery performed on morbidly obese individuals to achieve weight loss. Established procedures include Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, laparoscopic adjustable gastric band, biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch and sleeve gastrectomy.

sublevels.name: Fistula Creation
sublevels.description: An arteriovenous fistula creation is a surgical procedure performed by a vascular surgeon to create a connection between an artery and a vein. The fistula is usually placed on the forearm or upper arm; however, it may also be placed on the leg.

sublevels.name: Abdominal Surgery
sublevels.description: Surgery of gastrointestinal and endocrine organs like tract, liver, pancreas and endocrine organs, including very specialized procedures.

sublevels.name: Thoracic Surgery
sublevels.description: Thoracic surgery focuses on treating conditions of the body's thorax (chest) area, including the esophagus, lungs, mediastinum (the area between the lungs), trachea, and diaphragm. Thoracic surgeons treat the following conditions: Chest wall tumors. Emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, and other end-stage lung-diseases.

sublevels.name: Trauma Surgery
sublevels.description: Trauma surgery is a surgical specialty that utilizes both operative and non-operative management to treat traumatic injuries, typically in an acute setting. Trauma surgeons generally complete residency training in general surgery and often fellowship training in trauma or surgical critical care.

sublevels.name: Plastic Surgery
sublevels.description: Plastic surgery is a surgical specialty involving the restoration, reconstruction or alteration of the human body. It can be divided into two main categories: reconstructive surgery and cosmetic surgery.

sublevels.name: Reconstructive Surgery
sublevels.description: Reconstruction is the process of surgically rebuilding damaged tissue. This procedure restores the original form and function to tissues damaged through traumatic events such as motor vehicle accidents or substantial burns. Reconstruction can also restore form and function to tissue damaged through a surgery performed to treat another disease.

sublevels.name: Hand Surgery
sublevels.description: Hand surgery deals with both surgical and non-surgical treatment of conditions and problems that may take place in the hand or upper extremity (commonly from the tip of the hand to the shoulder) including injury and infection. Hand surgery may be practiced by post graduates of orthopedic surgery and plastic surgery.

sublevels.name: Aesthetic Surgery
sublevels.description: Aesthetic Surgery is a component of Plastic Surgery which applies surgical procedure to improve someone’s appearance.

sublevels.name: Health Care
sublevels.description: Health care is the discipline concerned with the provision and delivery of health services to a patient population by personnel in professional and allied health occupations.

sublevels.name: Speech and Language Therapy
sublevels.description: Speech and language therapy provides treatment, support and care for children and adults who have difficulties with communication, or with eating, drinking and swallowing. Speech and language therapists (SLTs) are allied health professionals. They work with parents, carers and other professionals, such as teachers, nurses, occupational therapists and doctors.

sublevels.name: Health Informatics
sublevels.description: Health informatics  is a multidisciplinary field that uses health information technology in delivery, management and planning  of health care services. It deals with the resources, devices, and methods required to optimize the acquisition, storage, retrieval, and use of information in health and bio-medicine.

sublevels.name: Quality of Life Research
sublevels.description: Quality of life is the standard of health, life satisfaction, life chances, and happiness experienced by individuals or groups. It implies the lack or the availability of various social and economic opportunities, rights and entitlements, equity, security that affect the life, health and happiness of people. The concept includes physical, emotional, social and psychological parameters.

sublevels.name: Disability Studies
sublevels.description: Disability Studies is an interdisciplinary field that studies the meaning, nature and consequence of disability. Disability is understood as a social construct, as opposed to impairment of a person's mind or body.

sublevels.name: State of Health
sublevels.description: Illness: is the response of person to disease, which is based on the person's perception…… symptom.  Wellness (health): is a status in which individual is capable of meeting the minimum physical, psychological and social requirements of appropriate functioning.

sublevels.name: Happiness Economics
sublevels.description: Happiness economics is the formal academic study of the relationship between individual satisfaction and economic issues such as employment and wealth.

sublevels.name: Genetic Service
sublevels.description: Genetic services are provisions to diagnose and advise individuals with risk factors for genetic disorders. Individuals with family members who have such disorders are often at risk of developing the disorder themselves. Genetic services include genetic testing and genetic counselling. Patient education often has a prominent role.

sublevels.name: Genetic Counseling
sublevels.description: Genetic counselling is an educational process that aims to inform and advise patients and relatives at risk of a genetic condition about the nature of the disorder, the probability of developing it and the risk of passing it on to future generations. Individuals can then make informed decisions about available testing, health management, treatment, and family planning options.

sublevels.name: Genetic Testing
sublevels.description: Genetic testing involves the detection of specific alleles, mutations, genotypes or karyotypes that are associated with heritable traits, diseases or predispositions to disease for the individual or their descendants. Genetic testing may also be used as a method for the determination of parentage or ancestry.

sublevels.name: Patient Education
sublevels.description: Patient education is the procedure in which individuals with health occupations impart information to patients about their own health status and needs. Patient education aims to enable patients to improve their own health by changing their health-related behaviours. Education can be therapeutic or used for disease prevention.

sublevels.name: Emergency Services
sublevels.description: Emergency services and rescue services are organizations that ensure public safety, security, and health by addressing and resolving different emergencies.

sublevels.name: Midwifery
sublevels.description: Midwifery deals with the normalcy of pregnancy while acknowledging the vulnerability associated with the reproductive process. To be distinguished from obstetrics, which deals with problems of pregnancy and birth.

sublevels.name: General Practice and Family Medicine
sublevels.description: General practice / family medicine is defined as the medical specialty that manages common and long-term illnesses in children and adults, focusing on overall health and well-being.

sublevels.name: Occupational Therapy
sublevels.description: Occupational therapy (OT) is the use of assessment and intervention to develop, recover, or maintain the meaningful activities, or occupations, of individuals, groups, or communities. It is an allied health profession performed by occupational therapists and occupational therapy assistants (OTA). OTs often work with people with mental health problems, disabilities, injuries, or impairments.

sublevels.name: Practice and Hospital Management
sublevels.description: Hospital Management is the process where healthcare providers effectively and efficiently administer everything from patient registration to appointment scheduling, document management, consultation management, lab management, drug safety, report generation, staff management, outpatient management, and more.

sublevels.name: Chiropractic Medicine
sublevels.description: Chiropractic is a form of alternative medicine concerned with the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of mechanical disorders of the musculoskeletal system, especially of the spine. Chiropractic medicine is based on the link between the alignment of the spine and the function of the body.

sublevels.name: Occupational Health
sublevels.description: Occupational health deals with all aspects of health and safety in the workplace and has a strong focus on primary prevention of hazards.

sublevels.name: Health Policy
sublevels.description: Health policy is the set of decisions and plans, developed by governmental or nongovernmental agencies, designed to promote specific health-care objectives. Policies can be directed at individuals, physicians, pharmaceutical companies, or health-care systems. Examples include tobacco control policies and those designed to promote equal opportunites to access care.

sublevels.name: Health Economics
sublevels.description: Health economics is a branch of economics concerned with issues related to efficiency, effectiveness, value and behavior in the production and consumption of health and healthcare.

sublevels.name: Palliative Care
sublevels.description: Palliative care is the set of medical interventions to alleviate symptoms, most frequently pain, associated with a medical condition. The main goal of palliative care is to reduce and prevent patient suffering. Unlike therapeutics, palliative care does not aim to cure the underlying disease. Palliative care is an interdisciplinary medical caregiving  approach that improves the quality of life of patients and their families facing the problems associated with life-threatening illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by means of early identification and impeccable assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, physical, psychosocial, and spiritual.

sublevels.name: Nursing
sublevels.description: Nursing encompasses autonomous and collaborative care of individuals of all ages, families, groups and communities, sick or well, and in all settings. Nursing includes the promotion of health, prevention of illness, and the care of ill, disabled and dying people. Advocacy, promotion of a safe environment, research, participation in shaping health policy and in patient and health systems management, and education are also key nursing roles. Nursing is the most diverse of all health care professions. Nurses practice in a wide range of settings but generally nursing is divided depending on the needs of the person being nursed.  The major populations are:  communities/public family/individual across the lifespan adult-gerontology pediatrics neonatal women's health/gender-related mental health informatics (eHealth) acute care hospitals ambulatory settings (physician offices, urgent care settings, camps, etc) school/college infirmaries

sublevels.name: Nursing Research
sublevels.description: Nursing research develops knowledge about health and the promotion of health over the full lifespan, care of persons with health problems and disabilities, and nursing actions to enhance the ability of individuals to respond effectively to actual or potential health problems. provides evidence used to support nursing practices.

sublevels.name: Nursing Education
sublevels.description: Formal learning and training in the science of nursing. This includes the functions and duties in the physical care of patients, and a combination of different disciplines that both accelerates the patient's return to health and helps maintain it. License and Certifications Associate degree nursing programs Baccalaureate nursing program Advanced practice nurses: RegisteredNs who specialize in one of several fields, which include nurse practitioner (NP), certified nurse midwife (CNM), certified registered nurse anesthetist (CRNA), and clinical nurse specialist (CNS).

sublevels.name: Learning Disabilities Nursing
sublevels.description: Learning disability nursing ensures that the needs of adults and children with learning disabilities are met, helping them to maintain their physical and mental health and supporting them with daily activities. Learning disability nurses help people with learning disabilities to live as independently as possible and may teach them the skills required to find work. Learning disability nurses may work in a range of settings, including people's homes, workplaces, hospitals and prisons.

sublevels.name: Geriatric Care
sublevels.description: Geriatric Care is a specialty that focuses on health care of elderly people. It aims to promote health by preventing and treating diseases and disabilities in older adults. Gerontological nurses work in collaboration with older adults, their families, and communities to support healthy aging, maximum functioning, and quality of life. This population tend to have more comorbidities such as high blood pressure, diabetes, heart conditions, etc. Gerontological nursing draws on knowledge about complex factors that affect the health of older adult

sublevels.name: Nursing Ethics
sublevels.description: Ethical values are essential for all healthcare workers. Ethical practice is a foundation for nurses, who deal with ethical issues daily. Ethical dilemmas arise as nurses care for patients. These dilemmas may, at times, conflict with the Code of Ethics or with the nurse's ethical values. Nurses are advocates for patients and must find a balance while delivering patient care. There are four main principles of ethics: autonomy, beneficence, justice, and non-maleficence

sublevels.name: Adult Nursing
sublevels.description: Adult Nursing means the medical care for adults. (AB) Adult nurses plan and provide nursing care to adults suffering from a wide variety of medical conditions and illnesses, supporting their treatment, recovery and well-being.

sublevels.name: Nursing Management
sublevels.description: Nursing management consists of the performance of the leadership functions of governance and decision-making within organizations employing nurses. It includes processes common to all management like planning, organizing, staffing, directing and controlling. It is common for registered nurses to seek additional education to earn a Master of Science in Nursing or Doctor of Nursing Practice to prepare for leadership roles within nursing. Management positions increasingly require candidates to hold an advanced degree in nursing.

sublevels.name: Pharmacy
sublevels.description: Pharmacy is a branch of healthcare that deals with the preparation, dispensing, and proper use of medications to ensure the safe and effective treatment of patients. Pharmacists are healthcare professionals who specialize in pharmacy practice, working closely with patients, healthcare providers, and other stakeholders to optimize medication therapy and promote health.

data.name: Humanities and Social Sciences
data.description: Social sciences focuses on subjects like economics, psychology, and history, while the humanities explore philosophy, languages and literature, and the arts.

sublevels.name: Politics and International Studies
sublevels.description: The study and practice of international relations is interdisciplinary in nature, blending the fields of economics, history, and political science to examine topics such as human rights, global poverty, the environment, economics, globalization, security, global ethics, and the political environment.

sublevels.name: International Relations
sublevels.description: International Relations is the study of relations across boundaries of (nation) states including international political economy, foreign policy analysis, diplomacy, peace and conflict studies, development studies, international security studies, migration studies and more. (Sarah Roughley)

sublevels.name: Terrorism and Political Violence
sublevels.description: Political violence is the collective use of armed force to exercise power over others for some substantive end. Political violence includes state aggression; armed conflict; mass atrocity; and terrorism.

sublevels.name: Development Studies
sublevels.description: Development studies is an interdisciplinary field of study that examines the economic, social, and political processes involved in the transformation of societies and the improvement of human well-being. It explores theories, policies, and practices related to poverty reduction, sustainable development, inequality, governance, and the role of institutions in fostering inclusive and equitable growth.

sublevels.name: Development Policy
sublevels.description: Development policy encompasses all political, economic and social measures to help improve living conditions in developing countries in a sustainable way.

sublevels.name: Development Aid
sublevels.description: Development aid is a type of foreign/international/overseas aid given by governments and other agencies to support the economic, environmental, social, and political development of developing countries.

sublevels.name: Development Theory
sublevels.description: Development theory is a collection of theories about how desirable change in society is best achieved. Such theories draw on a variety of social science disciplines and approaches.

sublevels.name: Sustainability
sublevels.description: Sustainability is essentially the ability to endure, for example by exploiting resources in a way that does not deplete their future availability or unduly damage the wider environment. This concept has been incorporated in the idea of sustainable development.

sublevels.name: International Organization
sublevels.description: An international organization is a stable set of norms and rules meant to govern the behavior of states and other actors in the international system. Organizations may be established by a treaty or be an instrument governed by international law and possessing its own legal personality, such as the United Nations, the World Health Organization and NATO.

sublevels.name: Globalization
sublevels.description: Globalization is the process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments worldwide. Globalization has accelerated since the 18th century due to advances in transportation and communication technology. This increase in global interactions has caused a growth in international trade and the exchange of ideas, beliefs, and culture. Political globalization refers to the growth of the worldwide political system, both in size and complexity. That system includes national governments, their governmental and intergovernmental organizations as well as government-independent elements of global civil society such as international non-governmental organizations and social movement organizations. One of the key aspects of the political globalization is the declining importance of the nation-state and the rise of other actors on the political scene.

sublevels.name: Peace and Conflict Studies
sublevels.description: Peace and conflict studies

sublevels.name: Military and Defence Studies
sublevels.description: Military and Defence studies is the sub-discipline of Political Science and International Relations, focusing on theoretical and practical studies in strategy, military operations, command and leadership, security, and defence policy of a particular international organization, region or country.

sublevels.name: International Relations Theory
sublevels.description: International relations theories can help us understand the way the international systems work, as well as how nations engage with each other and view the world.

sublevels.name: Diplomacy
sublevels.description: Diplomacy refers to spoken or written speech acts by representatives of states (such as leaders and diplomats) intended to influence events in the international system. It is the main instrument of foreign policy and global governance which represents the broader goals and strategies that guide a state's interactions with the rest of the world. International treaties, agreements, alliances, and other manifestations of foreign policy are usually the result of diplomatic negotiations and processes.

sublevels.name: International Security Studies
sublevels.description: International Security Studies is a sub-field within the wider discipline of international relations that studies organized violence, military conflict, national security, and international security.  It studies the measures taken by states and international organizations, such as the United Nations, European Union, and others, to ensure mutual survival and safety.  It covers areas such as security studies, strategic studies, and peace studies.

sublevels.name: Regionalism
sublevels.description: In international relations, regionalism is the expression of a common sense of identity and purpose combined with the creation and implementation of institutions that express a particular identity and shape collective action within a geographical region.

sublevels.name: Foreign Policy
sublevels.description: A state's foreign policy or external policy (as opposed to internal or domestic policy) is its objectives and activities in relation to its interactions with other states, unions, and other political entities, whether bilaterally or through multilateral platforms. A government's foreign policy may be influenced by domestic considerations, the policies or behaviour of other states, or plans to advance specific geopolitical designs.

sublevels.name: International Political Economy
sublevels.description: International Political Economy examines the interplay between politics and economics on a global scale, analyzing how political institutions, economic systems, and international relations shape global economic outcomes.

sublevels.name: Political Science
sublevels.description: Political science is the study of the theory and practice of politics at the local, national, and global level. It asks fundamental questions about the nature of power, and analyses political activities, thoughts, and behaviours, as well as systems and processes of governance.

sublevels.name: Political Sociology
sublevels.description: Political sociology is the study of power and the relationship between societies, states, and political conflict. It is a broad subfield that straddles political science and sociology, with “macro” and “micro” components.

sublevels.name: Area Studies
sublevels.description: Area studies are interdisciplinary fields of research and scholarship pertaining to particular geographical, national/federal, or cultural regions.

sublevels.name: Conflict and War
sublevels.description: War is an intense armed conflict between states, governments, societies, or paramilitary groups such as mercenaries, insurgents, and militias. It is generally characterized by extreme violence, destruction and mortality, using regular or irregular military forces.

sublevels.name: Party Research
sublevels.description: Party Research studies political parties, their organization, behavior, and role in the political system, including their impact on elections, governance, and public policy.

sublevels.name: Third Sector Research
sublevels.description: The third sector includes charities, social enterprises and volunteer groups, and aims to deliver essential services, help to improve people's well-being and contributes to economic growth.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Political Insitutions
sublevels.description: Political institutions can be defined as entities within a society that create, enforce, and make laws.  For example, the court system is a political institution, so is a head of state or head of government.  Political parties and unions are also considered political institutions.

sublevels.name: Research on Associations
sublevels.description: Associations are groups of persons banded together for a specific purpose.

sublevels.name: Research on Nationalism, Racism, Antisemitism and Extremism
sublevels.description: Racism on Nationalism, Racis, Anti-Semitism and Extremism examine the ideologies and practices that promote racial discrimination and national superiority, exploring their historical development and impact on societies and politics.

sublevels.name: Comparative Politics
sublevels.description: Comparative politics is a field in political science characterized either by the use of the comparative method or other empirical methods to explore politics both within and between countries.

sublevels.name: Urban Politics
sublevels.description: Urban politics is politics in and about cities. This term refers to the diverse political structure that occurs in urban areas where there is diversity in both race and socioeconomic status. City governments search for an equilibrium in their relations with the external environment.

sublevels.name: Democracy
sublevels.description: Democracy is a form of government in which the people have the authority to deliberate and decide legislation, or to choose governing officials to do so.

sublevels.name: Federalism
sublevels.description: Federalism is a combined and compound mode of government that combines a general government (the central or "federal" government) with regional governments (provincial, state, cantonal, territorial, or other sub-unit governments) in a single political system, dividing the powers between the two.

sublevels.name: Human Rights Policy
sublevels.description:
Politics and human rights is a subdiscipline that examines how human rights impacts  politics and also studies the role of human rights in relation to the politics of different regions of the world.

Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of race, sex, nationality, ethnicity, language, religion, or any other status. Human rights include the right to life and liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, freedom of opinion and expression, the right to work and education, and many more.  

International human rights law lays down the obligations of Governments to act in certain ways or to refrain from certain acts, in order to promote and protect human rights and fundamental freedoms of individuals or groups. International human rights law is the primary framework for specifying exact human rights obligations, especially for State Parties. There is increasing focus on the growing number of responsibilities accruing to non-state actors, particularly private actors.

sublevels.name: Middle Eastern Politics
sublevels.description: Middle Eastern Politics studies the political systems, movements, and conflicts in the Middle East, focusing on issues such as governance, regional dynamics, and international relations.

sublevels.name: Identity Politics
sublevels.description: Identity Politics involves the political mobilization and advocacy based on social identities, such as race, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity, aiming to address issues of representation, rights, and social justice.

sublevels.name: Politics and Religion
sublevels.description: Politics and Religion examines the interactions between religious beliefs, institutions, and political systems, exploring how religion influences political behavior, policy, and governance.

sublevels.name: Political Science of Religion
sublevels.description: Religious Political Science may involve, but are not limited to, those concerning freedom of religion, applications of religious law, and the right to religious education.

sublevels.name: Politics and Gender
sublevels.description: Politics and Gender examines the influence of gender on political behavior, representation, and policy-making, as well as the impact of political structures on gender equality and identity.

sublevels.name: Electoral Politics
sublevels.description: The study of elections and electoral systems.

sublevels.name: European Politics
sublevels.description: European politics is the study of political institutions, decision‑making processes, and power relations within and between the countries of Europe, including the governance structures of the European Union.

sublevels.name: British Politics
sublevels.description: British politics is the study of the political institutions, actors, and decision‑making processes of the United Kingdom, including its constitutional framework, parties, and systems of governance.

sublevels.name: European Union Politics
sublevels.description: Politics of the European Union

sublevels.name: Russian and Post-Soviet Politics
sublevels.description: Russian and Post-Soviet Politics is were political organizations and governmental bodies of the former Russian Empire, primarily associated with the Russian Revolution, which gave the name to the latter state of the Soviet Union.

sublevels.name: German Politics
sublevels.description: Germany is a democratic and federal parliamentary republic, where federal legislative power is vested in the Bundestag (the parliament of Germany) and the Bundesrat (the representative body of the Länder, Germany's regional states).

sublevels.name: Political Theory
sublevels.description: Political Theory involves the analysis and interpretation of political ideas, concepts, and ideologies, exploring fundamental questions about power, justice, rights, and the state.

sublevels.name: Critical Theory
sublevels.description: Critical Theory is a philosophical method and tradition that has its origins in Marx and Marxisms, especially of the Frankfurt School theorists.

sublevels.name: Political Ethics
sublevels.description: Political ethics is the practice of making moral judgements about political action and political agents.

sublevels.name: History of Political Thought
sublevels.description: History of Political Thought examines the development and evolution of political ideas, theories, and philosophies throughout history, exploring their impact on political systems and societies.

sublevels.name: Constructivism Theory in Political Science
sublevels.description: Constructivism Theory in Political Science posits that international relations and political outcomes are shaped by social constructs, such as identities, norms, and beliefs, rather than solely by material factors.

sublevels.name: Transcultural Comparative Political Theory
sublevels.description: Transcultural Comparative Political Theory examines political ideas and theories across different cultures, comparing and contrasting them to understand diverse political thought and practices.

sublevels.name: Executive Politics
sublevels.description: Exectutive politics studies the actions and power of heads of governments, including scholarship on the American presidency and also comparative executives, governors, bureaucracies, mayors, and other executives.

sublevels.name: African Politics
sublevels.description: African politics encompasses the diverse range of political systems, processes and challenges found across the continent, shaped by historical, cultural and socio-economic factors. It involves the governance structures, power dynamics and policy-making processes that reflect the continent's ongoing pursuit of democratic governance, economic development and regional integration.

sublevels.name: Asian Politics
sublevels.description: Asian Politics is a sub-discipline within political science that focuses on political systems of the region, transnational and strategic relations within Asia, as well as political developments within Asia.

sublevels.name: Chinese Politics
sublevels.description: Chinese Politics is a sub-discipline within political science that focuses on the political system of the the People's Republic of China, transnational and strategic relations with other countries, as well as political developments within China.

sublevels.name: Political History
sublevels.description: Political History studies the development and impact of political systems, institutions, leaders, and movements over time, focusing on how political events shape societies and governance.

sublevels.name: Political Leadership
sublevels.description: Political Leadership examines the roles, behaviors, and impact of individuals who hold positions of authority in political systems, including their decision-making processes and influence on governance.

sublevels.name: Methodology of Political Science
sublevels.description: The methods and ways in which political science is studied. This can be both quantitative and qualitative, including statistics and discourse research.

sublevels.name: Political Education
sublevels.description: Political Education involves the teaching and learning of political knowledge, skills, and values, aiming to develop informed and engaged citizens capable of participating in democratic processes.

sublevels.name: American Politics
sublevels.description: American Politics studies the political system of the United States, including its institutions, processes, behavior, and policies, as well as the historical and contemporary issues shaping American governance.

sublevels.name: Latin American Politics
sublevels.description: Since the 1980s, presidential and general elections have been held in many countries in Latin America, and the election systems based on the multi-party system has taken root in these countries. At present, nearly all of the 33 Latin American and Caribbean countries have established democratic governments.

sublevels.name: US Politics
sublevels.description: US politics refers to the political entities and processes which comprise government at all levels and all branches, including the Presidency, Congress, and the judicial system in the United States of America.

sublevels.name: Canadian Politics
sublevels.description: The politics of Canada function within a framework of parliamentary democracy and a federal system of parliamentary government with strong democratic traditions.[1] Canada is a constitutional monarchy, in which the monarch is head of state. In practice, the executive powers are directed by the Cabinet, a committee of ministers of the Crown responsible to the elected House of Commons of Canada and chosen and headed by the Prime Minister of Canada.

sublevels.name: Legislative Politics
sublevels.description: Legislative Politics examines the functioning, behavior, and decision-making processes of legislative bodies, including the roles of legislators, committees, and political parties in lawmaking.

sublevels.name: Political Ideology
sublevels.description: Political Ideology refers to a set of beliefs and values about the goals and organization of society, guiding political behavior and policy preferences, including ideologies such as liberalism, conservatism, and socialism.

sublevels.name: Public Policy
sublevels.description: Public Policy examines the executive branch of government, looking at its policies as well as those of political institutions and governance of the public sector. (Sarah Roughley)

sublevels.name: Policy Formulation
sublevels.description: It is the process of arriving at statements by organizing policy resources and supporting information to convert ideas into solutions that are practically implementable to deal with certain activity or address challenges evolved therewith and which are in the direction of the policy objectives.

sublevels.name: Agenda Setting
sublevels.description: The political process in which policies and policy issues are prioritized and considered for action by governments. It can be influenced by numerous factors, including the public, the media, policymakers and interest groups.

sublevels.name: Policy Adoption
sublevels.description: The stage in the policy-making process in which a policy or course of action is agreed upon in order to achieve a particular policy goal. Policy adoption is a part of the decision to choose policy alternatives after the policy formulation process. Mostly, the policy adoption process is influenced by internal and external determinants, often called policy diffusion. These determinants are each associated with elements that influence a government's decision to adopt a policy.

sublevels.name: Policy Implementation
sublevels.description: Implementation of policy by state and non-state actors on a global, regional and municipal scale. Policy implementation literature typically distinguishes between top-down and bottom-up approaches. The public sector generally, and national governments in particular, no longer detain a monopoly on policy implementation. Different agencies and levels of government can be involved in the implementation of policies and initiatives, representing diverse and often conflicting interests. Indeed in many cases, policies are not implemented by those who design it, and sometimes they are pursued by actors or stakeholders from outside the public administration.  Successful policy implementation is largely dependent on the government and other actors having the right tools at hand to identify the nature and dimensions of those challenges and to formulate and design adequate policy responses to address them.

sublevels.name: Policy Evaluation
sublevels.description: Policy evaluation examines the content, implementation, merit, worth and impact of policies.

sublevels.name: Comparative Public Policy
sublevels.description: An area of study that analyses and compares public policy across different systems, institutions, countries or governments.

sublevels.name: Migration Policy
sublevels.description: The study of government policies, statements, decisions, orders, and/or laws and regulations, regarding the selections, admission, settlement and deportation of foreign citizens residing in the country.

sublevels.name: Energy System Transformation
sublevels.description: The study of the policies concerning the shift from non-renewable to renewable energy sources. This often includes studying the governance and adoption of new technologies.

sublevels.name: Urban Policy
sublevels.description: The study of policies aimed at influencing the development of towns and cities, as well as their inhabitants.

sublevels.name: Public Management
sublevels.description: Public management is an area of political science that studies the way government programmes are managed

sublevels.name: Public Accounting
sublevels.description: Public accounting refers to a business or individual who helps a range of clients, from individuals to corporations, prepare financial documents. Certified public accountants, or CPAs, act as a third party to review the financials of a company for public disclosure.

sublevels.name: Organization Theory
sublevels.description: Organizational theory refers to a series of interrelated concepts that involve the sociological study of the structures and operations of formal social organizations. Organizational theory also seeks to explain how interrelated units of organization either connect or do not connect with each other.

sublevels.name: Privatisation
sublevels.description: Privatization refers to the transfer of government service or assets to the private sector. The assets owned by the government may be sold to the private sector or statutory restrictions on competition between publicly and privately owned enterprises may be lifted.

sublevels.name: Lobbying
sublevels.description: Lobbying” means communicating with any official in the legislative or executive branch for the purpose of attempting to influence legislative or administrative action or a ballot issue.

sublevels.name: Performance Management
sublevels.description: Performance management is an ongoing process of communication between a supervisor and an employee that occurs throughout the year, in support of accomplishing the strategic objectives of the organization.

sublevels.name: Public-Private Partnership
sublevels.description: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are a mechanism for government to procure and implement public infrastructure and/or services using the resources and expertise of the private sector.

sublevels.name: Governance and Government
sublevels.description: Government refers to the offices, departments and groups of people who control a political unit. Governance refers to the systems and processes by which those people act, operate and make policies and decisions.

sublevels.name: Global Governance
sublevels.description: Global governance refers to the complex of institutions, mechanisms, relationships, and processes between and among states, nonstate actors, markets, citizens, and organizations that articulate collective interests on the global plane, establish rights and obligations, and mediate differences.

sublevels.name: Civil Service/Bureaucracy
sublevels.description: The civil service is a collective term for a sector of government composed mainly of career civil servants hired rather than appointed or elected, whose institutional tenure typically survives transitions of political leadership. The term bureaucracy refers to a complex organization that has multilayered systems and processes. The systems and processes that are put in place effectively make decision-making slow. They are designed to maintain uniformity and control within the organization.

sublevels.name: Non-Profit Organisations
sublevels.description: A nonprofit organization (NPO) or non-profit organization, also known as a non-business entity, or nonprofit institution, is a legal entity organized and operated for a collective, public or social benefit, in contrary with an entity that operates as a business aiming to generate a profit for its owners.

sublevels.name: Citizenship
sublevels.description: Citizenship is an allegiance of a person to a state. Each state determines the conditions under which it will recognize persons as citizens, and the conditions under which that status will be withdrawn.

sublevels.name: Social Sciences
sublevels.description: A collectivity of people sharing interactions, relations and networks, usually in a geographical or physical space and with similarity of purpose or life aims.

sublevels.name: Anthropology
sublevels.description: Anthropology is the study of humans, their close relatives and their cultural environment. Subfields of anthropology deal with hominin evolution and the comparative study of extant and past cultures.

sublevels.name: Physical-Biological Anthropology
sublevels.description: Deals with human evolution, variability and human adaptation to climatic and habitat changes.

sublevels.name: Environmental Anthropology
sublevels.description: Environmental anthropology is a sub-discipline of anthropology that examines the complex relationships between humans and the environments which they inhabit.

sublevels.name: Disaster
sublevels.description: A disaster is a serious problem occurring over a period of time that causes widespread human, material, economic or environmental loss which exceeds the ability of the affected community or society to cope using its own resources

sublevels.name: Sociocultural Anthropology
sublevels.description: Sociocultural anthropology, also known as cultural anthropology, is one of the four main subfields of anthropology. It is the study of human societies, cultures, and social behaviors, focusing on understanding the diversity of human customs, beliefs, practices, and institutions. Some key aspects of sociocultural anthropology: Participant Observation, Ethnographic Research, Cultural Relativism, Cross-Cultural Comparison

sublevels.name: Race and Ethnicity Studies
sublevels.description: Race and Ethnicity Studies is an interdisciplinary academic field that focuses on the study of race, ethnicity, and related issues. It emerged as a response to the civil rights movements in the United States during the mid-20th century. Race and Ethnicity Studies critically analyze the concepts of race and ethnicity as social constructs rather than biological realities. It explores how these categories are shaped by historical contexts, power dynamics, and cultural representations.

sublevels.name: Ritual Studies
sublevels.description: Ritual Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the diverse forms, functions, and meanings of rituals in human societies. It aims to understand the role of rituals in social cohesion, cultural expression, and individual and collective identity, drawing on theories and methods from anthropology, sociology, religious studies, and other disciplines.

sublevels.name: Feminist Anthropology
sublevels.description: Feminist anthropology is a subfield of anthropology that emerged in the late 20th century and is characterized by its focus on gender and the exploration of women's roles, experiences, and contributions in different societies and cultures. It seeks to address historical imbalances and biases in traditional anthropological research that often neglected or marginalized the study of women and their perspectives.

sublevels.name: Material Culture
sublevels.description: Material culture refers to the physical objects and artifacts that are created, used, and valued by a particular society or group of people. These objects are tangible and can include a wide range of items, such as tools, clothing, buildings, art, religious symbols, technology, household items, and more. Material culture is an essential aspect of anthropology and archaeology as it provides valuable insights into the beliefs, values, social structures, and everyday life of past and present societies.

sublevels.name: Structural Anthropology
sublevels.description: Structural Anthropology is a branch of anthropology that analyzes human culture and society in terms of underlying structures, such as myths, kinship systems, and rituals. It seeks to identify universal patterns and principles that govern human behavior and cultural expression, drawing on structuralist theory and methodology.

sublevels.name: Evolutionary Anthropology
sublevels.description: Evolutionary Anthropology is a subfield of anthropology that combines principles from evolutionary biology with the study of human biology, behavior, and culture. It focuses on understanding human evolution and the evolutionary processes that have shaped human traits and behaviors over time. Evolutionary anthropologists use a multidisciplinary approach, integrating data from genetics, paleontology, archaeology, primatology, and other fields to piece together the evolutionary history of our species.

sublevels.name: Human Behavioral Ecology
sublevels.description: Human Behavioral Ecology uses the principles of evolutionary theory to study cultural and human behavioral diversity.

sublevels.name: Political and Economic Anthropology
sublevels.description: The study of political and economic systems within societies. It examines how political institutions, power dynamics, and economic activities shape social life, organization, and cultural practices. Political and economic anthropologists often conduct ethnographic research to understand the complexities of governance, decision-making processes, resource distribution, trade, and economic exchange in different cultural contexts.

sublevels.name: Anthropology of Work
sublevels.description: The study of human work and labor practices within societies. It examines the cultural, social, economic, and historical aspects of work, including the organization of labor, division of tasks, and the meaning and significance of work in different cultural contexts.

sublevels.name: Marxist Anthropology
sublevels.description: Also known as Anthropology of Marxism or Marxist-oriented Anthropology, is a theoretical approach within the field of anthropology that applies Marxist principles and perspectives to the study of societies and cultures. It draws on the ideas and critiques of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, focusing on social class, political economy, and historical materialism to understand human societies and cultural practices.

sublevels.name: Social Movements
sublevels.description: A social movement is a loosely organized effort by a large group of people to achieve a particular goal, typically a social or political one.  This may be to carry out a social change, or to resist or undo one.  It is a type of group action and may involve individuals, organizations or both.

sublevels.name: Anthropology of the Arts
sublevels.description: Anthropology of art is a sub-field in social anthropology dedicated to the study of art in different cultural contexts. The anthropology of art focuses on historical, economic and aesthetic dimensions in non-Western art forms, including what is known as 'tribal art'

sublevels.name: Museum Anthropology
sublevels.description: Museum anthropology, also known as anthropological museology or ethnographic museum studies, is a subfield of anthropology that focuses on the study of museums and their roles in preserving, representing, and interpreting human cultures and societies. It involves the examination of museums as institutions and the way they collect, exhibit, and engage with cultural artifacts and ethnographic materials.

sublevels.name: Anthropological Theory
sublevels.description: Anthropological theory are analytical tools for explaining and making sense of broad and complex anthropological topics. Anthropological theory is used in all four subfields of anthropology. Cultural anthropology focuses on studying cultural diversity amongst human societies.

sublevels.name: Historical Anthropology
sublevels.description: Historical anthropology is a historiographical movement which applies methodologies and objectives from social and cultural anthropology to the study of historical societies.

sublevels.name: Humanistic Anthropology
sublevels.description: “Humanistic anthropology involves the recognition that professional inquiry takes places in a context of human value. The humanistic orientation is particularly concerned with the personal, ethical, and political choices facing humans.”

sublevels.name: Medical Anthropology
sublevels.description: Medical anthropology studies "human health and disease, health care systems, and biocultural adaptation".

sublevels.name: Psychological Anthropology
sublevels.description: It combines principles and methods from both psychology and anthropology to study the relationship between culture and individual psychology. It seeks to understand how culture influences human behavior, cognition, emotions, and mental processes, and how individual psychological characteristics, in turn, shape and interact with cultural practices and beliefs. Psychological anthropologists use a range of research methods, including participant observation, interviews, surveys, and psychological testing, to gather data and insights into the complex interactions between culture and psychology.

sublevels.name: Applied Anthropology
sublevels.description: Applied anthropology is the practical application of anthropological theories, methods, and practices to the analysis and solution of practical problems.

sublevels.name: Ethnology
sublevels.description: Ethnology is a branch of anthropology that focuses on the comparative and analytical study of cultures and societies. It involves the examination of cultural and social aspects of different human groups and communities, seeking to understand the similarities, differences, and patterns that exist across diverse cultures. Ethnology contributes to our understanding of human societies and cultures, shedding light on the complexities of human behavior and social organization across different historical periods and geographical regions.

sublevels.name: Anthropology of Education
sublevels.description: Educational anthropology, or the anthropology of education, is a sub-field of anthropology and is widely associated with the pioneering work of Margaret Mead and later, George Spindler, Solon Kimball, and Dell Hymes, and Jean Lave. As the name would suggest, the focus of educational anthropology is on education, although an anthropological approach to education tends to focus on the cultural aspects of education, including informal as well as formal education.

sublevels.name: Sociology
sublevels.description: Sociology is the study of social life, change, social hierarchies and divisions, organizations, networks, and social causes and consequences of human behavior. Sociology studies social statics and dynamics at the level of the family as well as at global levels.

sublevels.name: Sociology of the Body
sublevels.description: The study of representations and social uses of the human body in modern societies.

sublevels.name: Health, Medicine and Society
sublevels.description: This is an interdisciplinary topic of study in the social sciences deriving perspectives from clinical sociology, medical sociology, medical anthropology, clinical social work, mental health research, well-being studies and psychiatry. It provides social, ethical and historical analyses of medicine and health.

sublevels.name: Care Systems and Practices
sublevels.description: Care Systems and Practices is a field that investigates the organization, provision, and quality of care for individuals and groups, such as children, the elderly, and people with disabilities. This includes examining formal care systems like healthcare, social services, and long-term care, as well as informal care provided by families and communities.

sublevels.name: Ethical, Legal, and Social Aspects of Genetics
sublevels.description: Genetics and Society analyzes the social, ethical, and legal implications of genetic research and technologies, examining issues such as genetic privacy, discrimination, and the impact of genetic information on individuals and communities.

sublevels.name: Innovation and Medicine
sublevels.description: Innovation and Medicine is a field of study that examines the processes, practices, and implications of medical innovations, exploring the social, ethical, and technological aspects of medical advancements and their impact on healthcare delivery and patient outcomes.

sublevels.name: Global Health
sublevels.description: Global health is the health of the populations in the worldwide context;[1] it has been defined as "the area of study, research, and practice that places a priority on improving health and achieving equity in health for all people worldwide"

sublevels.name: Sociology of Culture
sublevels.description: Sociology of Culture examines the ways in which culture influences social life, including the production, dissemination, and consumption of cultural goods, as well as the role of cultural norms and values in shaping social behavior.

sublevels.name: Sociology of the Arts
sublevels.description: Sociology of the Arts is a subfield of sociology that focuses on the analysis of the social dimensions of artistic production, consumption, and appreciation. This includes the study of the social organization of artistic institutions, the role of cultural capital in shaping artistic tastes and preferences, and the impact of art on societal values and identities.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Literature
sublevels.description: The sociology of literature is an interdisciplinary subfield of the sociology of culture. It examines the relationship between literature and society by studying the social production of literature and its social implications. It analyses how literature reflects, influences, and is influenced by social structures, cultural norms, historical contexts, and the collective consciousness of a given society. This subfield of sociology explores how literary works, such as novels, poems, plays, and other forms of creative expression, can serve as a mirror of societal values, beliefs, and conflicts, while also shaping public discourse and contributing to social change. Scholars in this area may investigate topics such as the role of literature in constructing identities, representations of social issues, the reception and interpretation of literary texts by different social groups, and the impact of literary movements on social thought and movements.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Music
sublevels.description: Sociology of Music is a subfield of sociology that examines the social and cultural aspects of music, including the production, consumption, and distribution of music and the ways in which music shapes and is shaped by society. Key areas of study include the role of music in identity formation, social interaction, and political expression.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Film
sublevels.description: Sociology of Film is a branch of sociology that explores the social, cultural, and political dimensions of film-making and film consumption. This includes the study of the film industry, production techniques, audience reception, and the representation of social issues and identities in cinema.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Consumption
sublevels.description: Sociology of Consumption is a subfield of sociology that investigates the social and cultural aspects of consumer behavior, the meanings attached to goods and services, and the relationship between consumption patterns and social organization. This field examines the role of consumption in shaping social identities, values, and relationships, as well as the implications of consumer culture for sustainability, well-being, and social inequality.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Everyday Life
sublevels.description: Sociology of everyday life zeroes in on the mundane, daily activities and interactions that shape human experience. It's all about the routines, habits, and social norms that occur without much notice but profoundly influence our existence. From a casual chat with a neighbor to how we navigate public spaces, this branch of sociology digs into what makes the ordinary so significant.

sublevels.name: Animal Sociology
sublevels.description: Animal sociology studies the social behaviors, interactions, and structures within animal species. It looks at how animals form communities, communicate, establish hierarchies, and cooperate or compete.

sublevels.name: Urban Sociology
sublevels.description: Urban sociology is the sociological study of cities and urban life. One of the field’s oldest sub-disciplines, urban sociology studies and examines the social, historical, political, cultural, economic, and environmental forces that have shaped urban environments.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Architecture
sublevels.description: Sociology of architecture is the sociological study of the built environment and the role and occupation of architects in modern societies.

sublevels.name: Rural Sociology
sublevels.description: Rural sociology is a field of sociology traditionally associated with the study of social structure and conflict in rural areas.

sublevels.name: Social Structure
sublevels.description: Social Structure refers to the organized patterns of relationships and institutions that make up a society, influencing social behavior, roles, and hierarchies.

sublevels.name: Social Inequality
sublevels.description: Social inequality is the condition of unequal access to the benefits and rights of society. In a purely equal society, every citizen is equally able to contribute to the overall wellbeing of that society, and they are equally able to benefit from their membership within that society.

sublevels.name: Leisure Studies
sublevels.description: Leisure studies is a branch of the social sciences that focuses on understanding and analyzing leisure.

sublevels.name: Tourism Studies
sublevels.description: Tourism Studies treats its study and research area as a whole, where physical, economic, social and cultural aspects of tourism, tourist markets, and destinations are the main corner-stones of learning.

sublevels.name: Media Sociology
sublevels.description: The study of mass media, communication technologies, and their role in shaping and influencing society. It examines how media institutions, content, and communication processes interact with social structures, cultural norms, and individual behaviors. Media sociology explores a wide range of topics, including media effects, media consumption patterns, media representation, media production, media ownership, and the broader social implications of media technologies.

sublevels.name: Digital Sociology
sublevels.description: Digital Sociology is the study of the relationship between digital technologies, social processes, and human behavior. This field explores topics such as the impact of the internet and social media on social interactions, the digital divide, online privacy, and the role of digital technologies in shaping social institutions, identities, and inequalities.

sublevels.name: Media Research
sublevels.description: Media research involves the study of media's impact on social, physical, and psychological aspects of people's lives. It involves the study of information related to mass communication. Newspapers, magazines, radio broadcasts, and television are examples of mass media.

sublevels.name: Economic Sociology
sublevels.description: Economic sociology is a subfield of sociology that examines the social foundations and consequences of economic activities, institutions and systems, often exploring issues such as capitalism, markets, globalization, and the role of culture in economic behavior.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Work
sublevels.description: Denotes social relations, behaviors, experiences and normative codes around work and working lives of people in society. The sociology of work cross-cuts discussions on gender, age, ethnicity, education, race, migration and globalization.

sublevels.name: Sociology of the Financial Market
sublevels.description: Sociology of the Financial Market is a subfield of sociology that examines the social structures, interactions, and institutions within financial markets to understand how market participants and organizations influence economic transactions and outcomes. This field explores the relationships between social and economic factors in the functioning of financial markets and the impacts of financial events on society at large.

sublevels.name: Convention Theory
sublevels.description: Convention theory is a sociological framework that examines how social norms, conventions, and institutions shape individual and collective behavior, focusing on the social coordination of actions, the formation of expectations, and the evaluation of performance in various social contexts.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Knowledge and Discourse
sublevels.description: Sociology of knowledge and discourse explores the relationship between social structures, power dynamics, and the production and circulation of knowledge. It investigates how knowledge is shaped by and shapes social institutions, norms, and practices.

sublevels.name: Discourse
sublevels.description: Discourse is the study of language in use and broader social practices, examining how spoken and written texts are structured, produced, and interpreted in various contexts. It includes the analysis of communication beyond the sentence level, addressing aspects such as power relations, ideology, and identity.

sublevels.name: Sociological Theory
sublevels.description: Sociological theory is the body of ideas and frameworks that seek to explain the social world and its phenomena, often focusing on the interconnections between individuals, social structures, institutions, and cultural contexts.

sublevels.name: Comparative Sociology
sublevels.description: Comparative sociology involves comparison of the social processes between nation states, or across different types of society (for example capitalist and socialist). There are two main approaches to comparative sociology: some seek similarity across different countries and cultures whereas others seek variance.

sublevels.name: Cultural Sociology
sublevels.description: the sociological study of the historical processes involved in cultural phenomena (such as art, philosophy, and religion)

sublevels.name: Historical Sociology
sublevels.description: Historical sociology is a branch of sociology that examines social structures, processes, and institutions from a historical perspective, using both historical data and sociological theories to better understand how societies evolve and change over time.

sublevels.name: Societal Psychology
sublevels.description: Societal Psychology is a branch of psychology that studies the impact of socio-cultural and political factors on individual and group behavior. This field seeks to understand how broader societal contexts shape cognition, emotion, and motivation, as well as how psychological processes influence the development of social structures and cultural norms.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Family, Youth and Aging
sublevels.description: Subfields of sociology that look into sociology of childhood and youth, family relationships within and across generations, kinship, and sociology of late life and adulthood.

sublevels.name: Child and Adolescence Psychology
sublevels.description: Child and Adolescent Psychology is a specialized field within psychology that focuses on the study of psychological development and behavior during childhood and adolescence. It examines the cognitive, emotional, social, and physical aspects of development from infancy through adolescence.

sublevels.name: Childhood Studies
sublevels.description: Childhood studies or children's studies (CS) or Critical Childhood Studies is a multidisciplinary field that seeks to understand the experience of childhood, both historically and in the contemporary world. CS views childhood as "a complex social phenomenon"[1] with an emphasis on children's agency as social actors, and acknowledges that childhood is socially constructed as the concept of childhood is not universal.

sublevels.name: Well-Being
sublevels.description: Well-being is the experience of health, happiness and prosperity, a sense of purpose in life, high life satisfaction, and the ability to manage stress.

sublevels.name: Community Well-Being
sublevels.description: Community wellbeing is the combination of social, economic, environmental, cultural, and political conditions identified by individuals and their communities as essential for them to flourish and fulfill their potential.”

sublevels.name: Child Abuse and Neglect
sublevels.description: This is a transdisciplinary field covering all aspects of child protection, rights, and public health, social welfare and humanitarian aid directed to the protection of children from exploitation, abuse, mistreatment, in any sphere of life.

sublevels.name: Social Theory
sublevels.description: Social theory is a framework for understanding and explaining social phenomena, ranging from micro-level interactions to macro-level structures and processes. It integrates concepts from various disciplines, such as sociology, anthropology, and philosophy, to analyze and interpret the dynamics and patterns of human societies.

sublevels.name: Medical Sociology
sublevels.description: The social, cultural, and institutional factors that influence health, illness, healthcare systems, and the medical profession. It examines how social structures, cultural norms, economic systems, and power dynamics intersect with health-related issues, shaping individual experiences and broader health outcomes.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Organizations and Occupations
sublevels.description: Denotes the study of formal and informal structures created to carry out social functions and often with specific purposes, for example, economic, social, political, technical, and educational. Sociologists study how organizations are created, governed, the relations within and between organizations, and hierarchies embedded in them. Occupational sociologists study the development of and interactions within occupations and professions in a society.

sublevels.name: Sociological Methods
sublevels.description: Sociological methods refer to the techniques and approaches used by sociologists to collect, analyze, and interpret data in order to study social phenomena. These methods enable researchers to investigate and understand various aspects of society, such as social structures, institutions, behaviors, and processes.

sublevels.name: Computational Social Sciences
sublevels.description: Computational social science refers to the academic sub-disciplines concerned with computational approaches used to model, simulate, and analyze social phenomena. It focuses on investigating social and behavioral relationships and interactions through social simulation, modeling, network analysis, and media analysis.Social Networks aim to analyze the structure of whole social entities as well as a variety of theories explaining the patterns observed in these structures. The study of these structures uses social network analysis to identify local and global patterns, locate influential entities, and examine network dynamics.

sublevels.name: Discourse Research
