sublevels.description: Discourse research is a research approach in sociology that focuses on analyzing language use and communication practices to understand how meaning is constructed and power relations are enacted within social contexts. It examines the ways in which language, both written and spoken, shapes and is shaped by social structures, identities, and cultural norms.

sublevels.name: Mixed Methods
sublevels.description: Mixed methods in sociology refer to research approaches that integrate both quantitative and qualitative methods to gain a comprehensive understanding of social phenomena. Rather than relying solely on one type of data, mixed methods research combines numerical data and statistical analysis with qualitative data and interpretive analysis.

sublevels.name: Sociological Quantitative Methods
sublevels.description: Sociological quantitative methods are research techniques that analyze numerical data in order to understand social patterns, relationships, and trends. It encompasses methods such as surveys, experiments, and statistical analysis.

sublevels.name: Sociological Qualitative Methods
sublevels.description: Sociological qualitative methods refer to a range of research approaches used in sociology to gather and analyze qualitative data for the purpose of understanding social phenomena. These methods emphasize the collection of non-numerical, in-depth, and descriptive data to explore social processes, meanings, and experiences.

sublevels.name: Biographical Research
sublevels.description: Biographical research is a qualitative research approach aligned to the social interpretive paradigm of research. The biographical research is concerned with the reconstruction of life histories and the constitution of meaning based on biographical narratives and documents.

sublevels.name: Oral History
sublevels.description: Oral history is the collection and study of historical information about individuals, families, important events, or everyday life using audiotapes, videotapes, or transcriptions of planned interviews. These interviews are conducted with people who participated in or observed past events and whose memories and perceptions of these are to be preserved as an aural record for future generations.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Food and Nutrition
sublevels.description: The sociology of food and nutrition, or food sociology, concentrates on the myriad sociocultural, political, economic and philosophical factors that influence our food habits— what we eat, when we eat, how we eat and why we eat.

sublevels.name: Network Research
sublevels.description: Network Research involves the study of networks, including social, biological, and technological networks, focusing on their structure, dynamics, and impact on various phenomena.

sublevels.name: Public Sociology
sublevels.description: Public Sociology is a subfield of sociology that focuses on the engagement of sociological knowledge and methods with the public, aiming to address societal issues, promote public discourse, and empower social change. This includes collaboration with non-academic audiences, such as policymakers, activists, and communities.

sublevels.name: History of Sociology
sublevels.description: The history of sociology traces the development of sociological ideas, theories, and methods from their origins to the present day. This field examines the foundations of sociology as an academic discipline, its evolution over time, the contributions of key thinkers and scholars, and the impact of historical events and social contexts on the course of sociological inquiry.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Science
sublevels.description: Sociology of science examines the social processes, institutions, and dynamics involved in the production, dissemination, and reception of scientific knowledge, including the role of scientific communities, funding, and public perception of science.

sublevels.name: Deviance and Social Control
sublevels.description: Deviance is any behavior that violates the norms of a society. Crime is a form of deviance that is considered to be so serious that is penalized by local laws. Social control involves the ways in which societies try to control deviant behavior.

sublevels.name: Socio-Legal Studies
sublevels.description: Socio-Legal Studies is an interdisciplinary field that combines elements of sociology and law to examine the social and cultural aspects of legal systems, legal processes, and the relationship between law and society. It focuses on understanding how law operates in practice, how it shapes social behavior, and how social factors influence legal processes and outcomes.

sublevels.name: Courts
sublevels.description: Courts is the study of the structure, functioning, and development of legal institutions responsible for the administration of justice, including analyses of judicial decision-making, procedural aspects, and the role of courts in shaping social norms and policies.

sublevels.name: Human Rights
sublevels.description: Human rights are rights inherent to all human beings, regardless of race, sex, nationality, ethnicity, language, religion, or any other status. Human rights include the right to life and liberty, freedom from slavery and torture, freedom of opinion and expression, the right to work and education, and many more.

sublevels.name: Juries and Criminal Trials
sublevels.description: Juries and Criminal Trials is the study of the role of jurors and the jury system in the administration of criminal justice. This area of research explores topics such as jury selection, jury decision-making, the impact of evidence and persuasion on jury verdicts, and the effectiveness of juries in providing fair and impartial trials.

sublevels.name: Criminal Justice
sublevels.description: Criminal justice is the system of practices, institutions, and policies involved in maintaining social control, deterring crime, and sanctioning those who violate laws, including law enforcement, the courts, and correctional facilities.

sublevels.name: Administrative Justice
sublevels.description: Administrative justice is the branch of law that requires public institutions and officials (as well as private institutions performing public functions) to adhere to due process principles when making administrative decisions, or taking administrative actions.

sublevels.name: Gender, Sexuality and Law
sublevels.description: This subject area explores the intersections of gender, sexuality, and legal institutions. It examines how laws and legal practices impact the experiences, rights, and identities of individuals based on gender and sexual orientation and how these factors shape legal theory and policy.

sublevels.name: Gerontology
sublevels.description: Gerontolotgy comprises the sociological aspects of elderly individuals' lives. Furthermore it addresses cultural, psychological, cognitive, and biological aspects of ageing and an aging population.

sublevels.name: Biogerontology
sublevels.description: Biogerontology is the study of the biological basis of ageing and age-related diseases. It represents the step in research which aims primarily at achieving healthy old age accompanied by improved longevity.

sublevels.name: Social Justice
sublevels.description: Social justice is a concept of fair and just relations between the individual and society, as measured by the distribution of wealth, opportunities for personal activity, and social privileges.

sublevels.name: Intersectionality
sublevels.description: Intersectionality is a framework for understanding how various forms of social stratification—like race, gender, class, and others—overlap and intersect, creating complex and unique systems of discrimination and privilege. Coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, it emphasizes that people's experiences can't be understood by looking at social categories in isolation; instead, we need to consider how these categories interact and influence each other.

sublevels.name: Social and Cultural Geography
sublevels.description: Studies the cultural landscapes which are determined by societies developing out of their local landscapes, and those landscaped being shaped on the the other hand by the societies located there. Social/Cultural geography is a complex research field that encloses a variety of subfields such as political and gender studies, anthropology, and sociology.

sublevels.name: Gender Geography
sublevels.description: Gender geography seeks to analyze how gendered social processes are linked to space, place, and scale. In this discussion, gender is defined as a social construct mediated by various axes of power that include race, class, ethnicity, and sexuality.

sublevels.name: Political Geography
sublevels.description: Political geography is concerned with the study of both the spatially uneven outcomes of political processes and the ways in which political processes are themselves affected by spatial structures.

sublevels.name: Legal Geography
sublevels.description: Studies focuses on law/legal systems considering a spatial connection, and how social and cultural systems affect it.

sublevels.name: Medical Geography
sublevels.description: Medical geography focuses on patterns of disease and death—of how diseases spread, for example, and how variations in morbidity and mortality rates reflect local environments—and on geographies of health care provision.

sublevels.name: Geoinformatics
sublevels.description: Geoinformatics or Digital Geography is the science and technology dealing with the structure and character of spatial information, its capture, its classification and qualification, its storage, processing, portrayal and dissemination, including the infrastructure necessary to secure optimal use of this information.

sublevels.name: Criminology
sublevels.description: Criminology is a multidisciplinary field of study that focuses on the scientific examination of crime, criminal behavior, and the societal response to crime. It encompasses the analysis of the causes and consequences of crime, the study of criminal justice systems, and the development of strategies for crime prevention and control. Criminologists draw upon various disciplines such as sociology, psychology, law, economics, and statistics to gain a comprehensive understanding of crime and its impact on individuals and society.

sublevels.name: Crime Control and Security
sublevels.description: Crime control and security refers to the field of study within criminology that focuses on preventing and minimizing criminal behavior and ensuring public safety through various strategies, policies, and practices. It encompasses the examination of measures aimed at detecting, deterring, and responding to criminal activities while maintaining social order.

sublevels.name: Policing
sublevels.description: Policing ocuses on the study of law enforcement agencies, their practices, policies, and strategies for maintaining public order, preventing crime, and ensuring community safety. It examines the role of police officers, the organization and structure of police departments, and the relationships between the police and the communities they serve. Policing in criminology encompasses various aspects, such as community policing, police discretion, use of force, accountability, and the impact of policing on crime and public trust.

sublevels.name: Crime Prevention
sublevels.description: Crime prevention is a field of study that focuses on strategies, interventions, and policies aimed at reducing and deterring criminal behavior within communities and societies. It involves understanding the causes and risk factors of crime, as well as identifying effective measures to prevent criminal acts and promote public safety.

sublevels.name: Terrorism
sublevels.description: Terrorism refers to the use of violence, intimidation, or the threat of violence to create fear and panic in a population, typically for political, religious, or ideological purposes. It is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon with diverse motivations, methods, and actors involved.

sublevels.name: Penology
sublevels.description: Penology refers to the study of punishment and correctional systems as a means of controlling and preventing crime. It involves examining the theories, practices, and institutions involved in the management of offenders, their treatment, and the overall goal of maintaining social order.

sublevels.name: Crime and the Media
sublevels.description: The subfield of crime and media within criminology focuses on the intersection of crime and various forms of media, including news reporting, television, film, literature, social media, and the internet. It examines how crime is portrayed, represented, and perceived through these media channels and explores the influence of media on public understanding, attitudes, and responses to crime.

sublevels.name: Research Methods in Criminology
sublevels.description: Research Methods in Criminology involve the techniques and methodologies used to study crime, criminal behavior, and the criminal justice system, including qualitative and quantitative approaches.

sublevels.name: Ethnography
sublevels.description: In criminology, ethnography is employed to gain an in-depth understanding of criminal behavior, criminal subcultures, and the lived experiences of individuals involved in criminal activities. Ethnographic research typically involves direct observation, participant observation, interviews, and analysis of cultural artifacts.

sublevels.name: Quantitative Criminology
sublevels.description: Quantitative criminology is a subfield of criminology that utilizes quantitative research methods and statistical analysis to examine patterns, trends, and relationships related to crime and criminal behavior. It involves the collection and analysis of numerical data, such as crime rates, offender characteristics, and factors associated with criminal activities, to gain insights and make empirical assessments within the field of criminology.

sublevels.name: Crime and Society
sublevels.description: The subfield of crime and society within criminology examines the complex relationship between crime and various social factors, including cultural, economic, political, and demographic influences. It focuses on understanding how crime is shaped by social structures, norms, and inequalities, and how crime, in turn, impacts society. This subfield delves into the social causes and consequences of crime, as well as the social responses to crime, including policies, interventions, and social control mechanisms.

sublevels.name: Criminal Behavior
sublevels.description: Criminal behavior refers to actions or activities that are deemed illegal according to the laws of a particular jurisdiction. It encompasses a wide range of behaviors that violate legal norms and can include offenses such as theft, assault, fraud, drug trafficking, and many others.

sublevels.name: Deviance
sublevels.description: Deviance is a concept within criminology that refers to behavior that deviates from the social norms or expectations of a particular society or group. It involves actions, beliefs, or traits that are perceived as violating the established standards or values of a community. Deviance is a complex phenomenon that can encompass a wide range of behaviors, from minor rule-breaking to serious criminal acts.

sublevels.name: Biosocial Criminology
sublevels.description: Biosocial criminology is a subfield within criminology that seeks to understand criminal behavior by examining the interplay between biological, genetic, and environmental factors. It combines insights from biology, genetics, neuroscience, psychology, and sociology to provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex causes of criminal behavior.

sublevels.name: Sexual Offending
sublevels.description: Sexual offending within criminology refers to the study of crimes involving sexual acts that are non-consensual, exploitative, or otherwise violate the laws and norms related to sexual behavior. It examines the causes, patterns, consequences, and prevention of sexual offenses, as well as the treatment and management of offenders.

sublevels.name: Violence and Crime
sublevels.description: It examines the various forms of violence, including interpersonal violence, domestic violence, sexual violence, homicide, and collective violence such as riots or terrorism, and it encompasses a wide range of criminal acts, from property offenses like theft and burglary to offenses against persons like assault, robbery, and murder. Researchers in this area investigate the individual, social, and environmental factors that contribute to the occurrence of violent and criminal behaviors, and analyze the impact of violence and crime on victims, offenders, communities, and society as a whole.

sublevels.name: Critical Criminology
sublevels.description: Critical criminology is a subfield within the broader field of criminology that adopts a critical perspective to examine crime, law, and the criminal justice system. It emerged in the 1960s as a response to traditional criminological approaches that were seen as overly focused on individual pathology and social control. Critical criminologists aim to understand the structural and systemic factors that contribute to crime and deviance, emphasizing the importance of power, inequality, and social justice in shaping criminal behavior and responses to it.

sublevels.name: Green Criminology
sublevels.description: Green criminology is a specialized subfield within criminology that focuses on the study of environmental crimes, harms, and conflicts. It examines the criminal and harmful behaviors that have an impact on the environment, including illegal activities related to pollution, wildlife trafficking, illegal logging, hazardous waste disposal, and other forms of ecological destruction.

sublevels.name: Hate Studies
sublevels.description: Hate crime focuses on the study of criminal offenses committed against individuals or groups based on their perceived race, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, or other protected characteristics. Hate crimes are motivated by bias, prejudice, or hatred towards a particular group, and they have significant social and psychological impacts on both victims and communities.

sublevels.name: Ethnicity, Class, Gender and Crime
sublevels.description: This subfield explores the intersectionality of race, social class, gender, and their influence on crime and criminal justice. It recognizes that individuals experience crime and justice differently based on their race, socioeconomic status, and gender, and seeks to understand the complex dynamics and inequalities that exist within these intersections.

sublevels.name: Forensic Science
sublevels.description: Forensic science is a branch of science that encompasses the application of scientific principles and techniques to investigate crime scenes, analyze evidence, and aid in the resolution of legal matters. It involves the collection, preservation, examination, and interpretation of physical and biological evidence using various scientific disciplines.

sublevels.name: Forensic Medicine
sublevels.description: The branch of medicine dealing with the application of medical knowledge to establish facts in civil or criminal legal cases, such as an investigation into the cause and time of a suspicious death.

sublevels.name: Forensic Psychiatry
sublevels.description: Is a branch of psychiatry deling with the assessment and treatment of offenders in prisons, secure hospitals and the community with mental health problems. It requires a sophisticated understanding of the links between mental health and the law.

sublevels.name: Forensic Dentistry
sublevels.description: Forensic dentistry or forensic odontology is the application of dental knowledge to those criminal and civil laws that are enforced by police agencies in a criminal justice system. Forensic dentists are involved in assisting investigative agencies to identify recovered human remains in addition to the identification of whole or fragmented bodies; forensic dentists may also be asked to assist in determining age, race, occupation, previous dental history and socioeconomic status of unidentified human beings.

sublevels.name: Forensic Anthropology
sublevels.description: Forensic anthropology is a subfield of forensic science that applies principles and methods of biological anthropology to analyze human skeletal remains in the context of legal investigations. It involves the identification, examination, and interpretation of skeletal and anatomical evidence to establish the identity, age, sex, ancestry, stature, and potential cause of death of individuals. Forensic anthropologists also play a crucial role in the recovery and analysis of human remains in forensic contexts, such as crime scenes or mass disasters.

sublevels.name: Transnational Crime
sublevels.description: Transnational crime refers to criminal activities that transcend national boundaries and involve multiple countries. These crimes often exploit gaps in legal systems, utilize advanced technology, and take advantage of global networks to carry out illegal operations. Examples of transnational crime include human trafficking, drug smuggling, arms trafficking, cybercrime, money laundering, and terrorism.

sublevels.name: State Crime
sublevels.description: State crime refers to illegal or unethical actions committed by governments, government officials, or state institutions, which violate human rights, international law, or domestic laws. State crimes can involve a wide range of offenses, such as torture, genocide, war crimes, corruption, and political repression.

sublevels.name: Trafficking
sublevels.description: Trafficking refers to the illegal trade and transportation of goods, services, or individuals, often involving exploitation and coercion. It is commonly associated with activities such as human trafficking, drug trafficking, arms trafficking, and trafficking in wildlife.

sublevels.name: Borders and Migration
sublevels.description: Borders and migration in criminology refers to the study of crime, criminal behavior, and related issues in the context of borders, immigration, and the movement of people across national boundaries. It examines the social, economic, and legal factors that influence migration patterns, as well as the criminal activities and challenges that arise in the process. Here are five synonyms for borders and migration:

sublevels.name: War Crime
sublevels.description: War crimes focus on the study of criminal acts committed during armed conflicts or war. War crimes are defined as serious violations of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions and other international treaties. These crimes occur during both international and non-international armed conflicts and involve acts such as deliberate targeting of civilians, torture, sexual violence, unlawful killings, forced displacement, and the destruction of civilian infrastructure.

sublevels.name: Prison and Punishment
sublevels.description: Prison and punishment is a subfield within criminology that focuses on the study of correctional systems, incarceration, and the various methods used by societies to respond to and punish individuals who have been convicted of crimes. It involves examining the theoretical foundations, historical development, and practical implementation of imprisonment and other forms of punishment.

sublevels.name: Rehabilitation Psychology
sublevels.description: Rehabilitation psychology is a field of study that focuses on promoting the psychological well-being, functional independence, and quality of life of individuals with disabilities or chronic health conditions. It involves understanding the impact of physical, cognitive, emotional, and social limitations on individuals' functioning and developing interventions to enhance their adjustment, coping skills, and overall rehabilitation outcomes. Rehabilitation psychologists work collaboratively with individuals, their families, and healthcare professionals to facilitate the recovery process, improve functioning, and optimize participation in daily activities and society.

sublevels.name: Recidivism
sublevels.description: Recidivism refers to the tendency or likelihood of an individual who has previously engaged in criminal behavior to reoffend or commit another crime after completing their sentence or intervention program. It focuses on studying the patterns, factors, and dynamics associated with repeated criminal behavior.

sublevels.name: Prison Policy
sublevels.description: Prison policy focuses on the examination and analysis of policies and practices related to the operation, management, and reform of prisons and correctional institutions. It involves studying various aspects such as sentencing, prison conditions, rehabilitation programs, parole systems, and the overall goals and effectiveness of incarceration.

sublevels.name: Probation
sublevels.description: Probation focuses on the study and practice of community-based correctional strategies aimed at rehabilitating and supervising individuals who have been convicted of crimes but have been given a suspended sentence or released on probation instead of serving time in prison. Probation involves monitoring and supporting offenders in the community, helping them reintegrate into society, and reducing the likelihood of reoffending.

sublevels.name: Organized Crime
sublevels.description: Organized Crime is the study of criminal enterprises that operate in a structured and hierarchical manner to engage in illegal activities for financial gain. Organized crime involves ongoing criminal enterprises with a high degree of organization, coordination, and longevity. These groups often specialize in activities such as drug trafficking, human trafficking, money laundering, extortion, racketeering, and other illicit endeavors.

sublevels.name: Crime and Technology
sublevels.description: This topic focuses on understanding how technological innovations, both positive and negative, impact criminal activities, crime prevention, and the criminal justice system. This subfield explores the use of technology in committing crimes, such as cybercrime and digital fraud, as well as the role of technology in crime detection, surveillance, and forensic analysis.

sublevels.name: Drugs
sublevels.description: The subfield of drugs within criminology focuses on the study of drug use, drug-related crime, drug policy, and the social and legal responses to drug-related issues. It examines the causes and consequences of drug abuse and addiction, the relationship between drugs and crime, drug markets, drug law enforcement, and the effectiveness of drug prevention and treatment programs.

sublevels.name: Weapons
sublevels.description: This subfield focuses on the study of various aspects related to weapons, including their types, characteristics, prevalence, usage patterns, legal regulations, and the implications of their involvement in criminal activities.

sublevels.name: Criminology Theory
sublevels.description: Criminology theory is a subfield within criminology that focuses on developing explanations and understanding the causes of criminal behavior, as well as the social, psychological, and environmental factors that contribute to crime. Criminology theories aim to provide frameworks for analyzing and predicting criminal behavior, informing the development of effective crime prevention strategies and criminal justice policies.

sublevels.name: Youth Offending and Juvenile Justice
sublevels.description: Youth offending refers to the involvement of those under the age of 18 in criminal or delinquent behavior. It includes a range of behaviors, from minor offenses to more serious crimes, and it often involves individuals who have not yet reached the age of criminal responsibility in their respective jurisdictions. Juvenile justice refers to the system of laws, policies, and institutions that are designed to address and respond to youth offending. It encompasses the legal processes, rehabilitative measures, and social interventions aimed at preventing and reducing juvenile delinquency, promoting the well-being of young offenders, and ensuring public safety.

sublevels.name: Criminology in the Global South
sublevels.description: The subfield of criminology in the Global South focuses on the study of crime, criminal behavior, and criminal justice systems in countries located in the southern regions of the world, particularly in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean. This field examines the unique social, cultural, economic, and political factors that contribute to crime patterns and the administration of justice in these regions. It acknowledges the diversity and distinctiveness of crime-related issues faced by countries in the Global South and seeks to develop contextually relevant theories, policies, and practices to address them.

sublevels.name: Cybercrime
sublevels.description: Cybercrime involves understanding and analyzing offenses committed using computer systems, networks, or the internet. Cybercrime encompasses a wide range of illegal activities, including hacking, identity theft, online fraud, cyberbullying, computer viruses, and more. This subfield focuses on examining the causes, consequences, and prevention of cybercriminal behavior.

sublevels.name: Asian Criminology
sublevels.description: study of criminology and criminal justice across Asia

sublevels.name: White Collar Crime
sublevels.description: White-collar crime is a category of nonviolent, financially motivated offenses typically committed by individuals or organizations in professional or business settings. It involves deceit, fraud, or violation of trust and are typically characterized by their nonviolent nature, reliance on manipulation, and pursuit of financial gain or economic advantage. This category encompasses a wide range of illegal activities, such as embezzlement, corporate fraud, insider trading, bribery, tax evasion, money laundering, and intellectual property theft.

sublevels.name: Corporate Crime
sublevels.description: Corporate crime focuses on the study of illegal or unethical behavior committed by corporations or individuals within corporate settings. It examines white-collar crimes such as fraud, embezzlement, bribery, insider trading, environmental violations, and other offenses committed for financial gain or to benefit the corporation.

sublevels.name: Financial Crime
sublevels.description: Financial crime refers to a category of criminal activities that involve fraudulent or illegal actions primarily motivated by financial gain. These activities typically target financial systems, institutions, or individuals, aiming to deceive, manipulate, or misappropriate financial resources for personal or organizational benefit.

sublevels.name: Gangs
sublevels.description: This subfield examines the formation, structure, behavior, and impact of gangs on individuals, communities, and the criminal justice system. This subfield seeks to understand the dynamics of gang involvement, motivations for joining gangs, gang violence, gang-related crime, and the social and economic factors that contribute to the existence and persistence of gangs.

sublevels.name: Victimology
sublevels.description: Victimology is a subfield of criminology that focuses on the study of victims of crime, their experiences, and the impact of victimization. It explores various aspects related to victims, such as their characteristics, vulnerabilities, coping mechanisms, the dynamics of victim-offender relationships, and the social, psychological, and physical consequences of victimization.

sublevels.name: History of Criminology
sublevels.description: This topic focuses on the historical development, evolution, and significant milestones of the discipline itself. It examines the influential theories, key thinkers, historical events, social and cultural contexts, and paradigm shifts that have shaped the field of criminology over time.

sublevels.name: Science and Technology Studies
sublevels.description: Science and technology studies, or science, technology and society studies (both abbreviated STS) is the study of how society, politics, and culture affect scientific research and technological innovation, and how these, in turn, affect society, politics and culture.

sublevels.name: Information and Communication Technologies (ICT)
sublevels.description: Information and communications technology (ICT) is an extensional term for information technology (IT) that stresses the role of unified communications[1] and the integration of telecommunications (telephone lines and wireless signals) and computers, as well as necessary enterprise software, middleware, storage and audiovisual, that enable users to access, store, transmit, understand and manipulate information.

sublevels.name: Gender and ICT
sublevels.description: Gender and ICT refers to the study of the relationship between gender and information and communication technologies, exploring the ways in which these technologies affect and are affected by gender roles, relationships, and inequalities. This area of research investigates topics such as digital access, digital literacy, technological innovation, and online gender-based harassment.

sublevels.name: Digital Culture
sublevels.description: Digital culture is the relationship between people and the use of technology. It describes how digital media and technology have shaped our everyday lives and interactions with society, people and work.

sublevels.name: Information Studies
sublevels.description: Information studies is a multidisciplinary field that explores how people create, collect, organize, and access information. It encompasses areas such as library science, data science, information management, and information technology.

sublevels.name: Human-Computer Studies
sublevels.description: "Human-Computer Studies" typically refer to interdisciplinary fields of study that examine the interaction and relationship between humans and computers, including aspects of design, usability, interface development, and more.

sublevels.name: Emerging Technologies
sublevels.description: Emerging technologies are technologies whose development, practical applications, or both are still largely unrealized. These technologies are generally new but also include older technologies finding new applications. Emerging technologies are often perceived as capable of changing the status quo.

sublevels.name: Technological Innovation
sublevels.description: A technological innovation is a new or improved product or process whose technological characteristics are significantly different from before. Implemented technological product innovations are new products (product innovations) or processes in application (process innovations) that have been brought to market.

sublevels.name: Social Robotics
sublevels.description: The field of social robotics concentrates on the development and design of robots which interact socially with humans, but sociality between robots (e.g., in multirobot systems) is not part of the field.

sublevels.name: Technoscience
sublevels.description: In common usage, technoscience refers to the entire long-standing global human activity of technology combined with the relatively recent scientific method that occurred primarily in Europe during the 17th and 18th centuries. Technoscience is the study of how humans interact with technology using the scientific method.

sublevels.name: Science, Technology and Society
sublevels.description: Science, Technology and Society (STS) is an interdisciplinary field that studies the conditions under which the production, distribution and utilization of scientific knowledge and technological systems occur; the consequences of these activities upon different groups of people.

sublevels.name: Global South and STS
sublevels.description: Global South and STS (Science and Technology Studies) is an interdisciplinary area of study that focuses on the relationships between science, technology, and society in the Global South, which includes developing and emerging countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It seeks to understand the ways in which science and technology are shaped by and impact socioeconomic, political, and cultural factors in these regions.

sublevels.name: Science and Technology Governance
sublevels.description: Science and Technology Governance explores the policies, regulations, and ethical considerations that guide the development and application of scientific research and technological innovations.

sublevels.name: Science Policy
sublevels.description: Science policy is concerned with the allocation of resources for the conduct of science towards the goal of best serving the public interest.

sublevels.name: Technopolitics
sublevels.description: Technopolitics (uncountable) Politics that relates to, or is driven by, modern technology.

sublevels.name: Gender and STS
sublevels.description: Gender and STS (Science, Technology, and Society) examines how gender influences and is influenced by scientific and technological developments, exploring issues of equity, representation, and impact.

sublevels.name: Postcolonial STS
sublevels.description: Postcolonial Science and Technology Studies (STS) critically analyzes the production, distribution, and consequences of scientific knowledge and technology in the context of historical colonialism and its aftermath. This interdisciplinary field explores the intertwined relationship between power, culture, and technology and seeks to decolonize the discourse on knowledge production.

sublevels.name: Chemistry in Society
sublevels.description: Chemistry in Society refers to the study and application of chemical principles, processes, and technologies to address various societal issues and challenges. It recognizes that chemistry plays a crucial role in shaping and impacting different aspects of our lives, from environmental concerns to health, energy, technology, and more.

sublevels.name: History of Chemistry
sublevels.description: The history of chemistry is rich, evolving from early discussions on the nature of matter in ancient Egypt and Greece, through to the emergence of alchemy, the development of the periodic table and quantum chemistry.

sublevels.name: Chemistry Policy
sublevels.description: "Chemistry policy" refers to the set of guidelines, regulations, and decisions made by governments, organizations, and international bodies to address various aspects of chemistry's impact on society, the environment, and human health. These policies aim to ensure the safe and responsible use of chemicals, promote scientific research and innovation, and mitigate potential risks associated with chemical substances.

sublevels.name: Chemistry Publishing
sublevels.description: Chemistry publishing and communication is the creation and dissemination of information that covers the discipline of chemistry. This topic covers, for example, editorial and publication processes (such as peer review), discussion of how information should be presented, methods of sharing data and the evolution of publishing as a business.

sublevels.name: Societal Outreach of Biology
sublevels.description: the efforts and activities within the field of biology that aim to engage with the general public, address societal issues, and communicate the relevance and implications of biological research to the broader community. It involves reaching out to non-scientific audiences, such as students, policymakers, the media, and the general public, to promote understanding, awareness, and ethical considerations related to biology.

sublevels.name: Bioethics
sublevels.description: Bioethics is the study of ethical, social, and legal issues that arise in biomedicine and biomedical research.

sublevels.name: Biolegalities
sublevels.description: Biolegalities explore the legal and ethical implications of biotechnological advancements, including issues related to genetic engineering, bioethics, and the regulation of biological research and applications.

sublevels.name: Bioeconomies
sublevels.description: Bioeconomy refers to an economic system that is based on the sustainable utilization of biological resources, including renewable resources from land and sea, as well as waste and byproducts, to produce food, energy, and industrial goods. It encompasses a wide range of sectors including agriculture, forestry, fisheries, biotechnology, and more.

sublevels.name: Posthumanism
sublevels.description: Posthumanism or post-humanism (meaning "after humanism" or "beyond humanism") is an idea in continental philosophy and critical theory responding to the presence of anthropocentrism in 21st-century thought

sublevels.name: Embodiment
sublevels.description: Embodiment is the concept that our physical bodies significantly shape and influence our experiences, thoughts, and behaviors. This interdisciplinary field involves the study of the relationship between the body and the mind in various domains such as psychology, philosophy, and anthropology.

sublevels.name: Bodies and Technology
sublevels.description: Bodies and Technology examines the interactions between human bodies and technological advancements, exploring how technology influences physical capabilities, identity, and societal norms.

sublevels.name: Body-Technology Studies
sublevels.description: Body-Technology Studies is an interdisciplinary area of research that investigates the complex interrelationship between human societies, cultures, and technological advancements. This field explores the social, ethical, and philosophical implications of technologies, including the impact on human values, well-being, and the future of humanity.

sublevels.name: Transhumanism
sublevels.description: Transhumanism is a class of philosophies that seek to guide us towards a posthuman condition. Transhumanism shares many elements of humanism, including a respect for reason and science, a commitment to progress, and a valuing of human (or transhuman) existence in this life.

sublevels.name: Expertise Studies
sublevels.description: The study of expertise is important for society in several ways. First, it sheds important light on learning and the acquisition of knowledge, which can be used to develop better methods of instruction and training.

sublevels.name: Expertise
sublevels.description: Expertise is special skill or knowledge that is acquired by training, study, or practice.

sublevels.name: Knowledge and Innovation
sublevels.description: Knowledge and Innovation has, as its objective, that of contributing through its basic and applied research to the generation of new knowledge on contemporary societies and the transformations taking place within them.

sublevels.name: Space Studies
sublevels.description: Space activity is a multi-disciplinary industry and coursework in space studies allows students to correlate the space experience to several fields of study. Often political, legal, ethical, historical, scientific and technological aspects are considered when studying space ventures.

sublevels.name: Societal Outreach of Physics
sublevels.description: Societal Outreach of Physics refers to efforts and activities aimed at increasing public understanding, appreciation, and engagement with the field of physics. This can include scientific communication, education, and collaboration with policymakers, industry, and other stakeholders to ensure that physics research and knowledge benefit society at large.

sublevels.name: Population and Demography
sublevels.description: Demography is the scientific study of human populations, focusing on their size, structure, distribution, and characteristics. It involves analyzing statistical data and social factors to understand population dynamics and how they change over time. Demography examines various aspects, including birth rates, death rates, migration patterns, age distribution, gender composition, socioeconomic status, and other demographic variables. The discipline of demography utilizes methods and tools from statistics, sociology, economics, geography, and other related fields to study and interpret population data. It provides valuable insights into population growth, mortality and fertility patterns, population aging, migration trends, and the implications of these factors for societies, economies, and public policy.

sublevels.name: Human Migration
sublevels.description: Human migration is the movement of people from one place to another intending to settle in a new geographic region.

sublevels.name: Migration and Health
sublevels.description: Migration and Health describes the overall condition (physical, mental, and social well-being) of an individual or a population who are on the move from one place to another with the intention to settle.

sublevels.name: Sociology of Migration
sublevels.description: The sociology of immigration involves the sociological analysis of immigration, particularly with respect to race and ethnicity, social structure, and political policy. Important concepts include assimilation, enculturation, marginalization, multiculturalism, postcolonialism, transnationalism and social cohesion.

sublevels.name: Life Course
sublevels.description: The entirety of an individual's life from birth to death and the typical set of circumstances an individual experiences in a given society as they age.

sublevels.name: Mortality and Longevity
sublevels.description: Longevity is how long a person can reasonably expect to live (i.e. human life expectancy); Mortality is the state or condition of being subject to death or the incidence of death within a population.

sublevels.name: Spatial Demography
sublevels.description: Spatial demography studies the population dynamics in relation to geographic locations and the spatial processes that influence population change.

sublevels.name: Fertility
sublevels.description: Fertility refers to the natural capability or capacity of an individual, couple, or population to produce offspring or children.

sublevels.name: Applied Demography
sublevels.description: Applied demography is a field of study that involves the practical application of demographic principles, methods, and techniques to real-world issues and problems. It focuses on using demographic data and analysis to inform and guide decision-making in various sectors, such as public policy, urban planning, healthcare, education, business, and social services.

sublevels.name: Aging Population
sublevels.description: Population aging refers to the process whereby the proportion of older individuals in a population increases over time, typically due to declining birth rates and increasing life expectancy. It is a demographic phenomenon that occurs when a society experiences a significant increase in the number and proportion of older adults relative to younger age groups.

sublevels.name: Social Policy
sublevels.description: Social policy refers to a set of principles, guidelines, laws, and programs implemented by governments and institutions to address social issues, improve the well-being of individuals and communities, and promote social justice and equality. It involves the formulation and implementation of policies and programs to tackle various social challenges and provide support and assistance to vulnerable populations.

sublevels.name: Education Policy
sublevels.description: Education policy is the study of governmental guidelines and decisions that govern the operation of education systems. This includes both childhood education and adult education.

sublevels.name: Citizenship Education
sublevels.description: Citizenship education, also known as civic education or civic engagement, refers to the process of equipping individuals with the knowledge, skills, and values necessary to actively participate in their communities, societies, and the broader world as informed and responsible citizens. It aims to foster an understanding of democratic principles, human rights, social justice, and civic responsibilities.

sublevels.name: Educational Inequality
sublevels.description: Critical Race Theory in Education is an interdisciplinary framework that examines how race and racism influence educational systems, policies, and practices

sublevels.name: Children, Youth and Family Policy
sublevels.description: A specific area of social policy that focuses on the well-being, protection, and support of children, youth, and families. It involves the development and implementation of policies and programs that address the unique needs and challenges faced by these vulnerable populations.

sublevels.name: Global Social Policy
sublevels.description: Global social policy is defined as the mechanisms, policies and procedures used by intergovernmental and international organisations, working with other actors, to both influence and guide national social policy and to provide for a supranational or global social policy.

sublevels.name: Comparative Social Policy
sublevels.description: Comparative Social Policy investigates the design, implementation, and outcomes of social policies and welfare systems across different countries or regions. This area of research aims to identify the factors that shape the development and effectiveness of social policies and examines the impact of these policies on social inequality, poverty, and well-being.

sublevels.name: Environmental Policy
sublevels.description: Studies the commitment of an organization or government to the laws, regulations, and other policy mechanisms concerning environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Welfare
sublevels.description: The term welfare refers to a range of government programs that provide financial or other aid to individuals or groups who cannot support themselves. Welfare programs are typically funded by taxpayers and allow people to cope with financial stress during rough periods of their lives.

sublevels.name: Social Economy
sublevels.description: The term 'social economy' refers to all business activities that are not only driven by a strong social mission but also intended to be economically viable.

sublevels.name: Public Administration
sublevels.description: The study of the implementation of government policies.

sublevels.name: Sport Science
sublevels.description: Sports science is a discipline that studies how the healthy human body works during exercise, and how sport and physical activity promote health and performance from cellular to whole body perspectives.

sublevels.name: Sports Medicine
sublevels.description: Sports Medicine is a subfield of medicine dealing with physical fitness and the treatment and prevention of injuries in sports and exercise. Although its origins lie in the clinical treatment of athletes, Sports Medicine traditionally also encompasses matters of performance physiology and methods of training control.

sublevels.name: Physiotherapy
sublevels.description: Physiotherapy is a health profession as well as a treatment method that focuses on the science of movement and helps people to restore, maintain and maximize their physical strength, function, motion and overall well-being by addressing the underlying physical issues. Physiotherapy aims at preventing injury and disability, managing acute and chronic conditions, Improving and maintaining optimal physical performance, Rehabilitating injury and the effects of disease or disability and Educating patients to prevent re-occurrence of an injury. For these purposes, Physiotherapy applies a variety of techniques, such as manual manipulation, electrical nerve stimulation, acupuncture, functional testing or provision of assistive, adaptive, supportive and protective devices and equipment.

sublevels.name: Fitness
sublevels.description: Fitness is generally understood as physical and also mental well-being. Altough being a vague concept without any measurable determinants, there are different factors contributing to overall fitness. In medicine, fitness refers to the physical, mental and emotional general condition of a person in relation to the performance demands placed on them from outside. From this perspective, fitness is affected by physical performance potential, intelligence, emotional stability, state of the immune system, reproducibility and Adaptability in case of lack of resources.

sublevels.name: Disability Sport
sublevels.description: Disability Sport refers to the aim to guarantee full participation of disabled persons (including physical and intellectual disabilities) into sport life, as practising sport not only covers the therapeutic and medical intentions generally defined as treatment, but also the social and educational aspects. Accordingly, disability sports or parasports, are sports played by persons with a disability (physical, mental, permanent and temporary). As many disabled sports are based on existing able bodied sports, modified to meet the needs of persons with a disability, they are sometimes referred to as adapted/adaptive sports.

sublevels.name: Sport Orthopaedics
sublevels.description: Sport Orthopaedics is a medical subspecialty of Orthopedics and Sports medicine. It focuses on the investigation, preservation, restoration and health care in general pertaining structures of the musculoskeletal system affected by athletic activity. Activities of Sport Othopedics include diagnosis of your injury or disorder, Treatment with medication, exercise, surgery or other treatment plans, rehabilitation through exercises or physical therapy to restore movement, strength and function, as well as prevention of injury or deceleration of progressing diseases.

sublevels.name: Sports Pharmacology
sublevels.description: Sports pharmacology includes study of the various aspects of the drug use and abuse (Doping) in sports and treatment of sports-related injuries. There are a variety of medications which are commonly used in a sports medicine setting. These are usually used to manage pain or in an attempt to reduce inflammation. Commonly abused agents in sports include anabolic–androgenic steroids and its analogs, blood, erythropoietin, growth hormone and its derivatives, nutritional supplements, creatine, amphetamines, beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), stimulants, and analgesics.

sublevels.name: Sports Economics
sublevels.description: Sports Economics is the study of issues of sports by means of economics, its methods and theoretical frameworks (heavily based on macroeconomics) as well as the study of economics problems in the context of sports. Sports Economics attempts to describe, explain and prognosticate actions by relevant parties and use the acquired knowledge technologically.

sublevels.name: International Sports Law
sublevels.description: International sports law (ISL) can be defined as the set of principles, rules, and processes that guarantee, relating to Sports and to ensure that these laws run smoothly to maintain the sports industry.

sublevels.name: Sport Sociology
sublevels.description: Sport Sociology is a discipline of sociology which in research and theory deals with Sport as a social phenomenon, the interrelations between individual actions and societal structures in sport, and the place of sports on society and the ever changing societal conditions. Like many other specialized subdisciplines of Sociology, Sport Sociology approaches its object of study strictly empirically and is oriented towards the formation of theory. Topics studied in Sport Sociology include communication and interaction on Sport and sport groups, social roles, expectations and attitudes towards sport, the process of socialisation in with and through sport, systems of values and norms, mass media representations and the social history of sport.

sublevels.name: Sport Career
sublevels.description: Sport Career primarily  refers to the career of an athlete, but might also refer to the occupational career of a person working in a wider context of sport. A career or professional career is the personal career of a person in his or her professional life. While the term career is generally understood to designate a change in qualification and income and is therefore related to social and economic upwards mobility, Sport Careers are similarly linked to the accumulation of accomplishments in sports and accompanying opportunities.

sublevels.name: Sports Communication
sublevels.description: Sports communication is an area of study that seeks to understand the relationship between communication processes and sport contexts. Communication processes refer to the creation and understanding of meaning through exchanging verbal and nonverbal messages. It can encompass the study of interpersonal and organizational communication between players, coaches, managers, referees, trainers and physiotherapists, and governing bodies, as well as communication between sports participants, fans, and the media and way in which sports are represented and communicated in the media. the methods used to study Sports Communication range from quantitative over qualitative approaches up to frameworks in critical and cultural studies. Studies in sports communication have addressed subjects such as audience reactions to mediated sporting contests; communication between coaches and athletes; media portrayals of athletes based on considerations such as gender, race, and nationality; and the professional routines of sports media practitioners.

sublevels.name: Sport Theory
sublevels.description: Sport Theory encompasses theoretical knowledge and analysis in the fields of biology, training theory, kinematics, as well as psychological, social and sociopolitical aspects of sport. In this regard, Sport theory draws on concepts from political sciences and sociological theories (such as theories of conflict and exchange, funcionalist, interactionalist, critical and feminist or figurational theories),  as well on concepts from philosophy end ethics to understand and explain the significance of sport in a more fundamental way.

sublevels.name: Sports Ethics
sublevels.description: Sports Ethics deals with any type of ethical issue, questions or problem in the context of Sport and attempts to suggest sensible courses of actions in order to alleviate or regulate these problems and establish ethical standards. Ethical issues in Sports commonly concern performance enhancing drugs (doping), Gender Discrimination, Fair Play, Responsibility for the performance, Fan Behaviour, Diversity or Protection of athletes health and safety.

sublevels.name: Sport Analytics
sublevels.description: Sport Analytics refers to the use of data and statistical methods to measure and evaluate performance for the purpose of being able to make decisions to improve performance and gain advantage over competing teams or athletes. Sport analytics is used during and prior to sport events and can inform players, coaches and other parties in aspects of game tactics, player fitness and health as well as the business of a sports organisation.

sublevels.name: Sport Technology
sublevels.description: Sport Technology is a area of study connecting sport science and engineering. Some subfields of Sport Technology are equipment and clothic technology, sports informatics, Sports measurement technology or Performance Diagnostics. Sport Technology might refer to any of the different uses of technical resources and devices in a sport context. Technology is applied to assist athletes, rehabilitate after injuries and increase performance, either during sport activities in the form of specialized gear or in preparation, evaluation and training (e.g. self monitoring, data bases, data evaluation). Technology is also applied for monitoring, broadcasting and to assist referees (usually in the form of computer software and cameras), as well as to manipulate the sporting environment (arena architecture, sport tracks/fields etc.)  Technology affects many aspects of sport from performance on and off the field to spectating and public profile. The use of technology in Sport is therefore ambivalent and might have positive and negative impact on sport from the perspective of athletes, officials or spectators

sublevels.name: Sport Psychology
sublevels.description: Sport Psychologyis is concerned with the preconditions and determining factors of the behaviour and experience of individuals (persons) in sport.  It aims at the adequate unterstanding of the behaviour and the experience of individuals in sport by describing and measuring consistency and variability, by offering explanations, as well as by determining their preconditions and possibilities to predict and shape its future course.  More specifically, Sport Psychology explores the processes of perception and decision making during sports games, the emergence or reduction of emotions (such as fear), the determining factors of an active lifestyle, the impact of sport on the development of children or the personality and group features of successful athletes and teams.

sublevels.name: Mental Training
sublevels.description: The term Mental Training is used to describe a variety of psychological methods, which aim at facilitating and improving performance, resilience, self-awareness, confidence or well-being by optimising social and communicative skills, cognitive skills or motivational and emotional processes.   In Sport Psychology, the narrow definition of Mental Training specifies it as training procedures for optimising the regulation of movement by conciously and repeatedly envisioning movement tasks or actions. Mental Training may also include techniques to regulate emotion (anger, fear, stress), motivation (will, achievement motivation) or perception (focus, concentration) and strengthen the athletes confidence in his or her capability. This may also include techniques that focus on coach-athlete or team interaction. Besides the long term systematic application of mental training, it is also used situationally in competition preparation or evaluation.

sublevels.name: Sport History
sublevels.description: Sport History aims at analyzing the sporting past by following socially relevant questions with the help of methodic instruments of historical science. It is concerned with historical events related to sports, the development of contemporary sport and its various cultural origins and predecessors, as well as with the shifting meaning of sport for individuals and social groups across time.

sublevels.name: Sport Training
sublevels.description: Sport Training refers to the special process of preparation of athletes and sports persons based on scientific principles aimed at improving and maintaining higher performance capacity in different sports activities. Training is designed to improve overall fitness and the abilities necessary to perform in a given sport, which might include strength training, practice of movement patterns, corrective and restorative exercises, conditioning and cardiovascular training, mental and psychological training and advise on nutrition. Sport training is usually an individual-specific process aided by scientific methods and findings and supported by a coaching person. It therefore involves some degree of education of the athlete and not only aims at improvement of physical fitness, but also at the acquisition of specific sports skills, improvement of tactical efficiency and mental abilities.

sublevels.name: Individual Sport
sublevels.description: Individual Sport is any sport which is practiced either by a single person (e.g. running) or by two opposing individuals (e.g. tennis). Competition in individual sports is also characterised by competing individuals rather than competing in teams. This allows athletes to aim for personal goals and has various effects on training strategies, tactics and the overall significance and prominence of individual athletes in individual sports.

sublevels.name: Team Sport
sublevels.description: Team sport includes any sport where individuals are organized into opposing teams of two or more members interacting directly and simultaneously in competition to win. The team members act together toward a shared objective and usually fulfill different roles and take positions with specific tasks and functions during a game. Examples of team sports are soccer, basketball, baseball, rugby or hockey.

sublevels.name: Sport Education and Didactics
sublevels.description: Sport Education is a curriculum and instruction model designed for delivery within physical education. Modifications can be made to suit each age category, activity or setting. It is most effective with games based activities and with participants who have a good base level of competence. Didactics refers to the science of teaching and instruction for any given field of study. Based on theoretical foundations, a didactic approach involves a very structured and informed approach to teaching and instruction.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Education
sublevels.description: Outdoor Education is an experiential learning approach that uses outdoor and natural settings to facilitate personal and social development, environmental awareness, and the acquisition of technical and practical skills. This field explores the theory, methods, and evaluation of outdoor education programs, as well as their role in fostering holistic and lifelong learning.

sublevels.name: Sports Biomechanics
sublevels.description: Sports Biomachanics refers to the description, detailed analysis and assessment of human movement during sport activities. Sport Biomachanics applies the laws of machanics to sport movements in order to explain how and why the human body moves in the way that it does and how the athletes body interacts with sports equipment and the environment during movement. Sport Biomachanics helps to gain unterstanding of athlete performance, as well as to minimise risk of injury, and increase performance. It usually includes detailed quantitative analysis of athletes movements by means of measurement, mathematical modelunf or computer simulation.

sublevels.name: Sports Neuromuscular Physiology
sublevels.description: Sports Neuromuscular Physiology is concerned with the physiology of the (human) Neuromuscular System, which links the central nervous system to the peripheral nervous system and is composed of a neural circuit including motor neurons in the spinal cord, sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglion, and skeletal muscle fibers. With regard to the context of sport, neuromuscular physiology is concerned with the relation between neuromuscular coupling, stimulation and muscle contraction during sport or exercise.

sublevels.name: Sport Kinematics
sublevels.description: Sport Kinematics is the study of the spatial and temporal expression of motion in sport. Kinematics is the study of the geometric and time-dependent aspects of motion. It describes different forms of motion, distinguishable with regard to the geometrical aspect (e.g. translation motion, rotation motion) and types of motion (e.g. uniform, non-uniform), regarding the temporal aspect. Kinematics therefore uses physical parameters such as velocity and acceleration, without analyzing causes (forces) and effects of motion.

sublevels.name: Fitness and Exercise Culture
sublevels.description: Fitness and Exercise Culture refers to the cultural and social factors and effects of fitness and physical exercise and is concerned with the ways in which people attribute meaning to sports activities through shared and culturally prescribed interpretative patterns.  It covers sports as a mass phenomenon and generally recognised and commerzialised types of sport, as well as communities of less popular and/or special and distinctive types of sport. This includes Lifestyle-, Health- and aesthetic aspects.

sublevels.name: Physical Recreation
sublevels.description: Physical recreation refers to a way of conducting sports or any kind of physical exercise for reasons of physical and mental regeneration and health, leasure, improvement of body awareness, social and team interaction, enhancement of self-discipline, perseverance and self-motivation as well as for personal experience of a sense of achievement. Most types of sport may be performed as physical recreation, however in a less organised, competitive and physically demanding way.

sublevels.name: Adventure Sports
sublevels.description: Types of sport performed mostly outdoors, in exceptional or hazardous environments, involving high degree of physical risk and bodily exertion due to height or speed. Characterised less by competition among athletes, than by great physical challenges, unusual experiences and/or highly spezialized athletic skills. Examples are Rock climbing, Mountainbiking, Canyoning, Surfing, Skydiving, Motocross etc.

sublevels.name: Outdoor Activity
sublevels.description: Outdoor activity refers to any leasure time activity characterised by being conducted outdoors, mostly in natural settings. They may be performed for physical or mental exercise, as well as for collective or personal enjoyment or enjoyment of the natural environment. Thus, the aspects of athleticism and competition are usually less emphasized. Examples are Bicycling, Fishing, Hiking, Hunting, canoeing etc.

sublevels.name: Sports Nutrition
sublevels.description: Sports Nutrition is an interdisciplinary field of study concerned with the understanding of the body's use of nutrients during athletic competition (and the need for nutritional supplements), as well as the practical use of proper nutrition and dietary supplements to enhance athletic performance. Works in the field of Sports Nutrition commonly apply knowledge nutrition science, dietology, biochemistry, exercise physiology, cell and molecular biology. For instance, studies in Sports Nutrition focus on the different types and quantities of fluids and food taken by an athlete, and also deals with the consumption of nutrients such as vitamins, minerals, supplements and organic substances that include carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

sublevels.name: Social Work
sublevels.description: Social work is a practice-based profession and an academic discipline that promotes social change and development, social cohesion, and the empowerment and liberation of people.

sublevels.name: Social Work Consulting
sublevels.description: Social work consulting is a field of study that focuses on providing expert guidance, advice, and support to individuals, organizations, and communities in addressing social issues and improving social work practices. Social work consultants apply their knowledge, skills, and experience to offer specialized insights, recommendations, and solutions to enhance the effectiveness and impact of social work interventions and programs.

sublevels.name: Domestic and Sexual Violence
sublevels.description: Domestic and sexual violence is a subfield of social work that focuses on addressing and preventing interpersonal violence within the context of intimate relationships and sexual encounters. It involves providing support, advocacy, and interventions for individuals and communities affected by domestic and sexual violence, as well as working towards creating social change to eliminate such violence.

sublevels.name: Social Work and Gender
sublevels.description: Social work and gender is a field of study within social work that focuses on understanding and addressing the ways in which gender influences social structures, relationships, and individual experiences. It involves promoting gender equality, challenging gender-based discrimination and oppression, and supporting individuals, families, and communities in achieving gender justice and empowerment.

sublevels.name: Social Work and Migration
sublevels.description: Social work and migration is a field of study within social work that focuses on understanding and addressing the unique challenges and needs of individuals, families, and communities affected by migration. It involves providing support, advocacy, and interventions to promote the well-being and social inclusion of migrants, refugees, and displaced populations.

sublevels.name: Theory and Method in Social Work
sublevels.description: Theory and method in social work refer to the foundational frameworks, concepts, and approaches used to understand and address social issues, as well as the systematic procedures and techniques employed in social work practice. Theories provide the theoretical underpinnings and conceptual frameworks that inform social work interventions, while methods outline the systematic steps and techniques used to implement these interventions and achieve desired outcomes.

sublevels.name: Social Area
sublevels.description: Social Area Analysis is a field of study within social work that focuses on examining and understanding the social dynamics, structures, and characteristics of specific geographic areas or communities. It involves analyzing various aspects of the community, such as its demographics, resources, social interactions, and community development. Social area analysis helps social workers gain insights into the unique challenges, strengths, and needs of communities, which can inform the design and implementation of effective social interventions.

sublevels.name: Critical Social Work
sublevels.description: Critical social work is a field of study within social work that focuses on challenging and addressing structural inequalities, power imbalances, and social injustices. It aims to promote social change, advocate for marginalized populations, and advance social justice through a critical examination of social systems, policies, and practices.

sublevels.name: Social Work Policy
sublevels.description: Social work policy is a field of study within social work that focuses on the development, analysis, and evaluation of social policies and their impact on individuals, families, groups, and communities. It involves examining the social, political, and economic factors that shape policies, advocating for social justice and equity, and promoting policies that address social issues and promote social well-being.

sublevels.name: Social Work Research
sublevels.description: Social work research is a specialized field of study that focuses on the systematic investigation of social issues, interventions, and policies to inform and improve social work practice. It involves the application of research methods and techniques to generate knowledge that contributes to evidence-based practice and social change.

sublevels.name: Social Work Education
sublevels.description: Social Work Education involves the academic and practical training of individuals to become professional social workers, focusing on skills, ethics, and knowledge required for social services.

sublevels.name: Social Work and Community Development
sublevels.description: Studies processes that help to develop local communities; it is a very much practice-orientated or applied discipline, based on sustainable development, economics, equality, social justice, resilience, and the work of social insitutions.

sublevels.name: Religion
sublevels.description: Religion is a range of social-cultural systems, including designated behaviors and practices, morals, beliefs, worldviews, texts, sanctified places, prophecies, ethics, or organizations, that generally relate humanity to supernatural, transcendental, and spiritual elements —although there is no scholarly consensus over what precisely constitutes a religion.

sublevels.name: Christianity
sublevels.description: Christianity is an Abrahamic monotheistic religion based on the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth.

sublevels.name: Black Theology
sublevels.description: Black theology refers to conceptions of the divine informed by the Black experience and tradition.

sublevels.name: Liberation Theology
sublevels.description: Liberation theology is a Christian theological approach emphasizing the liberation of the oppressed. It engages in socio-economic analyses, with social concern for the poor and political liberation for oppressed peoples and addresses other forms of inequality, such as race or caste.

sublevels.name: Christian Theology
sublevels.description: Christian theology is the theology of Christian belief and practice.[1] Such study concentrates primarily upon the texts of the Old Testament and of the New Testament, as well as on Christian tradition. Christian theologians use biblical exegesis, rational analysis and argument.

sublevels.name: Biblical Studies
sublevels.description: Biblical studies involves an in-depth, systematic analysis of each book of the Bible. It dives into matters such as authorship, canon, text, criticism, and interpretation

sublevels.name: Eschatology
sublevels.description: Eschatology concerns expectations of the end of the present age, human history, or the world itself. The end of the world or end times is predicted by several world religions (both Abrahamic and non-Abrahamic), which teach that negative world events will reach a climax. Belief that the end of the world is imminent is known as apocalypticism, and over time has been held both by members of mainstream religions and by doomsday cults. In the context of mysticism, the term refers metaphorically to the end of ordinary reality and to reunion with the divine. Various religions treat eschatology as a future event prophesied in sacred texts or in folklore.

sublevels.name: Ecclesiology
sublevels.description: Ecclesiology is the study of the Church, the origins of Christianity, its relationship to Jesus, its role in salvation, its polity, its discipline, its eschatology, and its leadership.  In its early history, one of the Church's primary ecclesiological issues had to do with the status of Gentile members in what had become the New Testament fulfilment of the essentially Jewish Old Testament church. It later contended with such questions as whether it was to be governed by a council of presbyters or a single bishop, how much authority the bishop of Rome had over other major bishops, the role of the Church in the world, whether salvation was possible outside of the institution of the Church, the relationship between the Church and the State, and questions of theology and liturgy and other issues. Ecclesiology may be used in the specific sense of a particular church or denomination's character, self-described or otherwise. This is the sense of the word in such phrases as Catholic ecclesiology, Protestant ecclesiology, and ecumenical ecclesiology.  The word ecclesiology was defined in the 19th century as the science of the building and decoration of church buildings and is still used in that sense in the context of architectural history.

sublevels.name: Feminist Theology
sublevels.description: Feminist theology is a movement found in several religions, including Buddhism, Hinduism, Sikhism, Neopaganism, Baháʼí Faith, Christianity, Judaism, Islam, and New Thought, to reconsider the traditions, practices, scriptures, and theologies of those religions from a feminist perspective.

sublevels.name: Christian Cultural Studies
sublevels.description: Christian culture generally includes all the cultural practices which have developed around the religion of Christianity. There are variations in the application of Christian beliefs in different cultures and traditions. Although theology can be an aspect of religious studies and religious studies can be an aspect of theology, these college degrees are distinct in important ways.
