It deals with economic structures of different transport systems, their socio-economic impact, demand and supply of transports, different transport models and the study of their capacity, effectiveness, frequency, environment and financing; cost benefit analysis, public and commercial transport planning, economics of and investments in transport infrastructure projects, transport data analytics, and transportation policy.

sublevels.name: Maritime Economics
sublevels.description: Maritime economics explains trade and economic aspects of commercial shipping, port operations, and how different types of shipping markets are organized and works, including demand and supply variations, reasons for sea transport, organization of sea transport, transport of bulk, general, merchant & specialized cargo, prices and freight rates determination, ship finance, market cycles, shipping companies risk and return on investment, how shipping company survive depressions, drivers in ship design, market forecasts, and environmental costs.

sublevels.name: Education Economics
sublevels.description: Education economics, or the economics of education, is the study of economic issues relating to education, including the demand for education, the financing and provision of education, and the comparative efficiency of various educational programs and policies.

sublevels.name: Public Economics
sublevels.description: Public economics (or economics of the public sector) is the study of government policy through the lens of economic efficiency and equity. Public economics builds on the theory of welfare economics and is ultimately used as a tool to improve social welfare. Welfare can be defined in terms of well-being, prosperity, and overall state of being.

sublevels.name: Public Choice and Political Economy
sublevels.description: Public choice, or public choice theory, is "the use of economic tools to deal with traditional problems of political science". Its content includes the study of political behavior. In political science, it is the subset of positive political theory that studies self-interested agents (voters, politicians, bureaucrats) and their interactions, which can be represented in a number of ways – using (for example) standard constrained utility maximization, game theory, or decision theory. Political economy approaches in general contend that the success or failure of public policies depends on political struggles, or the ability to neutralise political struggles, around resources.

sublevels.name: Public Finance
sublevels.description: Public finance is the study of the role of the government in the economy. It is the branch of economics that assesses the government revenue and government expenditure of the public authorities and the adjustment of one or the other to achieve desirable effects and avoid undesirable ones. The purview of public finance is considered to be threefold, consisting of governmental effects on: 1.	The efficient allocation of available resources; 2.	The distribution of income among citizens; and 3.	The stability of the economy.

sublevels.name: Fiscal Policy
sublevels.description: Fiscal policy refers to the use of government spending and tax policies to influence economic conditions, especially macroeconomic conditions. These include aggregate demand for goods and services, employment, inflation, and economic growth. Fiscal policy is one of the two main tools used by the government to influence the economy. The other is monetary policy.

sublevels.name: Socio-Economic Policy
sublevels.description: Social policy is concerned with the ways societies across the world meet human needs for security, education, work, health and wellbeing. Social policy addresses how states and societies respond to global challenges of social, demographic and economic change, and of poverty, migration and globalisation. Social policy is a plan or action of government or institutional agencies which aim to improve or reform society. The economy of governments covers the systems for setting levels of taxation, government budgets, the money supply and interest rates as well as the labour market, national ownership, and many other areas of government interventions into the economy.

sublevels.name: Economic Policy
sublevels.description: The economy of governments covers the systems for setting levels of taxation, government budgets, the money supply and interest rates as well as the labour market, national ownership, and many other areas of government interventions into the economy.  Most factors of economic policy can be divided into either fiscal policy, which deals with government actions regarding taxation and spending, or monetary policy, which deals with central banking actions regarding the money supply and interest rates.

sublevels.name: Microeconomics
sublevels.description: Microeconomics is a branch of mainstream economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources and the interactions among these individuals and firms.

sublevels.name: Social Choice and Welfare
sublevels.description: Social Choice and Welfare studies the methods and principles for aggregating individual preferences and making collective decisions, focusing on issues of fairness, efficiency, and social welfare.

sublevels.name: Voting
sublevels.description: Voting is when a group of people decide something by saying what they want. It can be for electing a leader or representative, passing a law, and other things. When people are done voting, the votes are counted (often by machines) and the winner is determined.

sublevels.name: General Equilibrium
sublevels.description: General equilibrium shows how supply and demand interact and tend toward a balance in an economy of multiple markets working at once. The balance of competing levels of supply and demand in different markets ultimately creates a price equilibrium.

sublevels.name: Economy-wide Country Studies
sublevels.description: Macroeconomics is a branch of economics that deals with the performance, structure, behavior, and decision-making of an economy as a whole—for example, using interest rates, taxes, and government spending to regulate an economy's growth and stability. This includes regional, national, and global economies.   Macroeconomists study topics such as GDP (Gross Domestic Product), unemployment (including unemployment rates), national income, price indices, output, consumption, inflation, saving, investment, energy, international trade, and international finance.

sublevels.name: Asian Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of Asia comprises about 4.7 billion people (60% of the world population) living in 50 different nations. Asia is the fastest growing economic region, as well as the largest continental economy by both GDP Nominal and PPP in the world.

sublevels.name: Middle Eastern/North African Economics
sublevels.description: Middle East and Northern Africa (MENA) encompasses the countries between Iran in the East and Tunisia and Morocco in the West. According to OPEC data, the MENA region holds more than half of the world's oil reserves, and two-fifths of the world's natural gas reserves. Due to the region's substantial petroleum and natural gas production, MENA is an important source of global economic and energy resources.

sublevels.name: Latin American/Caribbean Economics
sublevels.description: Latin America as a region has multiple nation-states, with varying levels of economic complexity. The Latin American economy is an export-based economy consisting of individual countries in the geographical regions of North America, Central America, South America, and the Caribbean.

sublevels.name: North American Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of North America comprises more than 596 million people (8% of the world population) in its 24 sovereign states and 15 dependent territories. It is marked by a sharp division between the predominantly English speaking countries of Canada and the United States, which are among the wealthiest and most developed nations in the world, and countries of Central America and the Caribbean in the former Latin America that are less developed. Mexico and Caribbean nations of the Commonwealth of Nations are between the economic extremes of the development of North America.

sublevels.name: African Economics
sublevels.description: Africa makes up around 20% of the earth's landmass, and is home to approximately 16% of the world's population. Nevertheless, Africa's economies account for just 3% of the world's GDP. In the past, economic ties between African nations and strong economies outside of Africa have been fundamentally exploitative.

sublevels.name: European Economics
sublevels.description: The economy of Europe comprises about 748 million people in 50 countries. The formation of the European Union (EU) and in 1999 the introduction of a unified currency, the Euro, brought participating European countries closer through the convenience of a shared currency and has led to a stronger European cash flow. The European Union is a unique global organisation, an entity forming one of the largest economies in the world. The European Union also “regulates” the global market by the single market.

sublevels.name: Industrial Organization
sublevels.description: Industrial organization is an analysis of factors, operational or otherwise, that contribute to a firm's overall strategy and product placement. It involves a study of different areas, from market power to product differentiation to industrial policy, that affect a firm's operations.

sublevels.name: Regulation and Industrial Policy
sublevels.description: Industrial policy can be defined as a statement stating the role of government in industrial development, the position of public and private sectors in industrialization of the country, the comparative role of large and small industries.

sublevels.name: Market Structure and Economic Design
sublevels.description: According to economic theory, market structure describes how firms are differentiated and categorized by the types of products they sell and how those items influence their operations. A market structure helps us to understand what differentiates markets from one another. Review of Economic Design comprises the creative art and science of inventing, analyzing and testing economic as well as social and political institutions and mechanisms aimed at achieving individual objectives and social goals.

sublevels.name: Economic History
sublevels.description: Economic history is the study of history using methodological tools from economics or with a special attention to economic phenomena.

sublevels.name: Financial History
sublevels.description: Financial History studies the development of financial systems, institutions, and markets over time, including the evolution of banking, investment, and monetary policies.

sublevels.name: Corporate History
sublevels.description: A corporate history is a historical account of a business or other co-operative organization. Usually it is produced in written format but it can also be published as audio or audiovisually.

sublevels.name: Quantitative Economics
sublevels.description: Quantitative economics is analyzis of economic issues, explore theories, and predict future conditions using statistical procedures and mathematical models.

sublevels.name: Experimental Economics
sublevels.description: Experimental Economics uses controlled experiments to study economic behavior and test economic theories, providing empirical insights into decision-making processes and market dynamics.

sublevels.name: Computational Economics
sublevels.description: Computational Economics is a field of research in which economists and computer scientists use software-based methods to solve analytical problems in order to make accurate predictions about the economy.

sublevels.name: Econometrics
sublevels.description: Econometrics is the application of statistical and mathematical methods to economic data. It aims to quantify economic relationships, test economic theories, and forecast future economic trends. By using statistical tools, econometrics helps in making informed decisions and policies based on empirical data. It combines economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference to analyze economic phenomena.

sublevels.name: Time Series Analysis
sublevels.description: A time series is a sequence of measurements performed at successive points in time. Time series can be used to derive models to predict future values based on previously observed values. Time series are used in statistics, signal processing, pattern recognition, econometrics, mathematical finance, weather forecasting, earthquake prediction, electroencephalography, control engineering, astronomy, communications engineering, and largely in any domain of applied science and engineering which involves temporal measurements

sublevels.name: Macroeconomics and Monetary Economics
sublevels.description: Monetary economics is the branch of economics that studies the different theories of money: it provides a framework for analyzing money and considers its functions (such as medium of exchange, store of value, and unit of account), and it considers how money can gain acceptance purely because of its convenience as a public good. The discipline has historically prefigured, and remains integrally linked to, macroeconomics. This branch also examines the effects of monetary systems, including regulation of money and associated financial institutions and international aspects.  Modern analysis has attempted to provide microfoundations for the demand for money and to distinguish valid nominal and real monetary relationships for micro or macro uses, including their influence on the aggregate demand for output. Its methods include deriving and testing the implications of money as a substitute for other assets and as based on explicit frictions.

sublevels.name: Regional Economics
sublevels.description: Regional Economics refer to the economic advantage of a geographical location and human activities of greatest height to contribute maximally to the general growth and prosperity of the region. Spatial economics is the study of how space (distance) affects economic behavior.

sublevels.name: Spatial Economics
sublevels.description: Spatial Economics studies the allocation of resources and economic activities across different locations, focusing on factors such as transportation, land use, and regional development.

sublevels.name: Heterodox Economics
sublevels.description: Heterodox economics is any economic thought or theory that contrasts with orthodox schools of economic thought, or that may be beyond neoclassical economics.

sublevels.name: Institutional and Evolutionary Economics
sublevels.description: Institutional economics focuses on understanding the role of the evolutionary process and the role of institutions in shaping economic behavior. Its original focus lay in Thorstein Veblen's instinct-oriented dichotomy between technology on the one side and the "ceremonial" sphere of society on the other. Evolutionary economics is a theory proposing that economic processes evolve and that economic behavior is determined both by individuals and society as a whole. The term was first coined by Thorstein Veblen (1857-1929), an American economist and sociologist.

sublevels.name: Agent-based Economics
sublevels.description: Agent-based computational economics (ACE) is the area of computational economics that studies economic processes, including whole economies, as dynamic systems of interacting agents. As such, it falls in the paradigm of complex adaptive systems.

sublevels.name: Feminist Economics
sublevels.description: Feminist economics is the critical study of economics and economies, with a focus on gender-aware and inclusive economic inquiry and policy analysis. Feminist economic researchers include academics, activists, policy theorists, and practitioners. Much feminist economic research focuses on topics that have been neglected in the field, such as care work, intimate partner violence, or on economic theories which could be improved through better incorporation of gendered effects and interactions, such as between paid and unpaid sectors of economies.

sublevels.name: Marxist Economics
sublevels.description: Marxian economics is a school of economic thought based on the work of 19th-century economist and philosopher Karl Marx. Marxian economics, or Marxist economics, focuses on the role of labor in the development of an economy and is critical of the classical approach to wages and productivity developed by Adam Smith.

sublevels.name: Demographic Economics
sublevels.description: Demographic economics is the use of population data as a way to study the patterns of behavior among groups of people that impact the economy. This is also why it is known as population economics. Demographics are statistics about groups of people that help to identify groups for tracking and research purposes.

sublevels.name: Gender Economics
sublevels.description: Gender economics is the study of how gender affects individuals' economic behavior, opportunities, and outcomes, incorporating the analysis of the impact of gender roles, discrimination, and policies on labor markets, income distribution, and resource allocation.

sublevels.name: Economics of Migration
sublevels.description: Economics of Migration studies the economic causes and consequences of migration, including the impact on labor markets, economic growth, and the distribution of resources.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Economics
sublevels.description: Behavioral Economics is the study of psychology as it relates to the economic decision-making processes of individuals and institutions. Behavioral economics is often related with normative economics. It draws on psychology and economics to explore why people sometimes make irrational decisions, and why and how their behavior does not follow the predictions of economic models.

sublevels.name: Political Economy and Economic Systems
sublevels.description: Political economy is an interdisciplinary branch of the social sciences. It focuses on the interrelationships of individuals, governments, and public policy. Political economists study how economic theories such as capitalism, socialism, and communism work in the real world. A political-economic system can be defined as the relationship between political and economic institutions in a particular country, as well as their policies. Market, command, and mixed economies are all examples of economic systems, and each of those can easily be influenced by politics.

sublevels.name: History of Economic Thought and Methodology
sublevels.description: Research in the History of Economic Thought and Methodology (RHETM) is a journal/book series dedicated to an interdisciplinary approach to a broad range of topics related to the history and methodology of economics.

sublevels.name: Transitional Economics
sublevels.description: The study of economies that move from one economic system to another. This is an area of study that developed following the end of the Soviet Union and the shift from centrally planned economies to market economies seen within the ex-Soviet states. Other countries that have also shifted economic systems, such as China and countries in South America, have also been areas of focus.

sublevels.name: Political Economy of Energy
sublevels.description: Political Economy of Energy studies all aspects of energy in relation to law, customs and government.

sublevels.name: Financial Economics
sublevels.description: Financial economics, also known as finance, is the branch of economics characterized by a "concentration on monetary activities", in which "money of one type or another is likely to appear on both sides of a trade". Its concern is thus the interrelation of financial variables, such as share prices, interest rates and exchange rates, as opposed to those concerning the real economy. It has two main areas of focus: asset pricing, commonly known as "Investments", and corporate finance; the first being the perspective of providers of capital, i.e. investors, and the second of users of capital. It thus provides the theoretical underpinning for much of finance.  The subject is concerned with "the allocation and deployment of economic resources, both spatially and across time, in an uncertain environment". It, therefore, centers on decision-making under uncertainty in the context of the financial markets, and the resultant economic and financial models and principles, and is concerned with deriving testable or policy implications from acceptable assumptions. It is built on the foundations of microeconomics and decision theory.  Financial econometrics is the branch of financial economics that uses econometric techniques to parameterize these relationships.

sublevels.name: Financial Services
sublevels.description: The financial services industry is a broad field of business and management research that encompasses organizations and institutions involved in the provision of financial products and services to clients. This includes banking, insurance, investment management, and other financial intermediation services. Research in this field may focus on the structure and organization of financial institutions, regulatory frameworks, financial markets and instruments, risk management, and the impact of technology and innovation on the industry. It may also explore the behavior of financial consumers and their decision-making processes, as well as the economic and social implications of financial services for individuals, businesses, and societies.

sublevels.name: Insurance
sublevels.description: The insurance industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the study of the insurance sector. This includes the analysis of various types of insurance products such as life insurance, health insurance, property and casualty insurance, and other specialized insurance products. Research in this field covers a range of topics, including the regulation of the industry, risk management, underwriting, claims processing, and actuarial science. Additionally, research may examine the impact of emerging technologies on the industry, the use of big data and analytics, and the role of insurance in broader economic and social contexts.

sublevels.name: Islamic Finance
sublevels.description: Islamic finance is a type of financing activities that must comply with Sharia (Islamic Law). The concept can also refer to the investments that are permissible under Sharia. The common practices of Islamic finance and banking came into existence along with the foundation of Islam.

sublevels.name: Household Finance
sublevels.description: The household finance industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the financial behavior of households, including their borrowing, saving, investment, and insurance decisions. The research in this field is concerned with understanding the factors that influence households' financial decisions and the consequences of those decisions for their financial well-being. This includes examining the impact of financial literacy and education, income and wealth, demographic factors, and social and cultural factors on household financial behavior. The household finance industry is interdisciplinary, drawing on insights from economics, psychology, sociology, and other fields to better understand the complex financial decisions made by households.

sublevels.name: Banking
sublevels.description: The banking industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on financial institutions that provide various banking services to individuals, businesses, and governments. It includes the study of banking operations, financial management, risk management, corporate governance, regulations, and innovations in the banking sector. Some of the key topics in banking industry research include the impact of technology on banking, financial regulation and compliance, financial risk management, asset and liability management, investment banking, retail banking, and financial inclusion. The banking industry is a critical component of the global economy, and research in this field can provide insights into economic growth, financial stability, and sustainable development.

sublevels.name: Capital Markets
sublevels.description: A capital market is a financial market in which long-term debt (over a year) or equity-backed securities are bought and sold, in contrast to a money market where short-term debt is bought and sold. Capital markets channel the wealth of savers to those who can put it to long-term productive use, such as companies or governments making long-term investments.

sublevels.name: Financial Crises
sublevels.description: A financial crisis is any of a broad variety of situations in which some financial assets suddenly lose a large part of their nominal value.

sublevels.name: Behavioral Finance
sublevels.description: Define behavioral finance as in research and practice Behavioral finance is an interdisciplinary field of study that combines principles of psychology and economics to understand how human behavior and emotions influence financial decisions and markets. In research and practice, behavioral finance aims to explain why people make irrational financial decisions, and how these decisions impact markets and the economy as a whole.  Behavioral finance researchers study various psychological and cognitive biases that affect financial decision-making, such as overconfidence, loss aversion, and herding behavior. They also examine the role of emotions, social norms, and cultural factors in shaping financial attitudes and behaviors.  In practice, behavioral finance is used to develop strategies and tools for improving financial decision-making and investment outcomes. This may include developing investment products that take into account investors' behavioral tendencies and preferences, or designing financial education programs that aim to overcome common cognitive biases and promote rational decision-making.  Overall, behavioral finance seeks to provide a more complete understanding of financial markets and investor behavior, with the goal of improving investment outcomes and reducing financial risk.

sublevels.name: Statistical Finance
sublevels.description: Statistical Finance applies statistical methods and models to analyze and predict financial markets, asset prices, and economic trends.

sublevels.name: Investments and Securities
sublevels.description: The Investments and Securities industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the analysis, management, and trading of financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, options, and other securities. The field encompasses a wide range of topics, including portfolio management, risk management, financial analysis, asset pricing, trading strategies, and market microstructure. It involves understanding the behavior of financial markets and the factors that influence their movements, as well as developing models and tools to help investors make informed decisions about their investments. Research in this field often involves the use of quantitative methods and may draw upon insights from economics, finance, and mathematics.

sublevels.name: Financial Econometrics
sublevels.description: Financial econometrics is the application of statistical methods to financial market data. Financial econometrics is a branch of financial economics, in the field of economics. Areas of study include capital markets, financial institutions, corporate finance and corporate governance. Topics often revolve around asset valuation of individual stocks, bonds, derivatives, currencies and other financial instruments.

sublevels.name: Resource and Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental and resource economics, a specialization option in the economic sciences major, applies economic and management decision tools to issues in forest management, water use, pollution, land use, fisheries, recycling, and hazardous wastes.

sublevels.name: Agricultural Economics
sublevels.description: Agricultural economics is an applied field of economics concerned with the application of economic theory in optimizing the production and distribution of food and fiber products. It involves studying the economic aspects of agricultural activities, including farming, food production, agribusiness, rural development, and natural resource management. Agricultural economists analyze and evaluate factors that influence agricultural markets, policies, and decision-making at various levels, from individual farms to national and international agricultural systems.

sublevels.name: Food Production
sublevels.description: Food production is the process of converting raw materials into finished food products. The finished food or converted food items are used either in homes or food processing industries. Food is vital for the human body to continue its basic life processes, providing energy and nutrition. Food production provides a stable source of employment, plays an important role in local economies, contributes to innovation in the food system, responds to increased demand for exports, contributes to food affordability, addresses consumer demand.

sublevels.name: Natural Resource Economics
sublevels.description: Natural Resource Economics is the study of how societies use and manage the Earth's natural resources—such as water, minerals, forests, and energy—in ways that balance economic needs with environmental sustainability.

sublevels.name: Environmental Economics
sublevels.description: Environmental economics is the study of the economics of ecological and environmental issues. It focuses on the monetary value of ecosystems and the costs and benefits of environmental policies.

sublevels.name: Energy Economics
sublevels.description: Energy economics studies human utilization of energy resources and the consequences of that utilization.

sublevels.name: Economic Development, Innovation and Growth
sublevels.description: Innovation has led to increased productivity even as the workweek became shorter and production less capital intensive over the last two centuries. Breakthrough innovations have been associated with increased productivity levels across firms and sectors, and positive macroeconomic impacts.

sublevels.name: Development Economics
sublevels.description: Development economics is a branch of economic study that focuses on improving fiscal, economic, and social conditions in developing countries.

sublevels.name: Development Finance
sublevels.description: Development finance is a subset of economics comprising hypotheses and practices on how to efficiently allocate resources towards economic and social transformation (development) of entire nations. It was born out of the challenge to promote the rapid economic transformation (development) of newly independent nations, and to reconstruct former industrial economies destroyed, physically and economically, by the two great wars of the twentieth century.

sublevels.name: Economics of Innovation
sublevels.description: Innovation economics is new, and growing field of economic theory and applied/experimental economics that emphasizes innovation and entrepreneurship.

sublevels.name: Economic Growth
sublevels.description: Economic growth is commonly measured in terms of the increase in aggregated market value of additional goods and services produced, using estimates such as GDP.

sublevels.name: Sustainable Growth
sublevels.description: Sustainable economic growth means maintaining growth without creating economic problems or complications. It's the practise of supporting long-term economic growth without depleting resources.

sublevels.name: Labor Economics
sublevels.description: Labor economics is the study of the labor force as an element in the process of production. The labor force comprises all those who work for gain within the labor market, whether as employees, employers, or as self-employed, but also the unemployed, who are seeking work.

sublevels.name: Trade Unions
sublevels.description: A trade union is "an organisation consisting predominantly of employees, the principal activities of which include the negotiation of rates of pay and conditions of employment for its members.

sublevels.name: Unemployment
sublevels.description: Unemployment, in the field of psychology, refers to the state of being without a paid job or occupation, despite actively seeking employment. It is a complex socio-economic phenomenon that can have significant psychological effects on individuals, including feelings of stress, anxiety, loss of self-esteem, and reduced well-being. Psychological research on unemployment explores the impact on mental health, coping strategies, job-seeking behaviors, and interventions to support individuals during this challenging period.

sublevels.name: Law and Economics
sublevels.description: The law and economics movement applies economic theory and method to the practice of law. It asserts that the tools of economic reasoning offer the best possibility for justified and consistent legal practice. It is arguably one of the dominant theories of jurisprudence.

sublevels.name: Economics of International Organizations
sublevels.description: Economics of International Organizations examines the economic roles, functions, and impacts of international institutions such as the IMF, World Bank, and WTO on global economic governance and development.

sublevels.name: Literature
sublevels.description: Literature is any collection of written work, but it is also used more narrowly for writings specifically considered to be an art form, especially prose fiction, drama, and poetry.

sublevels.name: Literary History
sublevels.description: Literary history is the development of writings in prose, poetry and drama over time. It focuses on specific literary movements and trends that characterized particular periods of literature.

sublevels.name: Contemporary Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works written in the modern, present-day period. Refers to literature from the second half of the twentieth century and texts written in the twenty-first century.

sublevels.name: Classical and Antique Literature
sublevels.description: Studies of literary works written in the ancient world. Usually refers to literature from ancient Greece, Rome and other ancient civilizations.

sublevels.name: Eighteenth-Century Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works produced between 1700 to 1799. Often also refers to the Long Eighteenth Century, which spans from the Glorious Revolution of 1688 to the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. Includes literature of the Enlightenment, satire, novels, travel writing, politeness and sentimental writing.

sublevels.name: Classics and Classicism
sublevels.description: The following of ancient Greek or Roman principles and style in art and literature, especially from the Renaissance to the 18th century. Generally refers to a high regard for a classical period.

sublevels.name: Goethe
sublevels.description: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749-1832) was a German writer, poet, playwright, and philosopher. He is considered one of the most prominent figures in German literature and a key representative of the Weimar Classicism movement. Goethe's works span various genres, including poetry, drama, fiction, and non-fiction, and his contributions have had a lasting impact on literature and cultural discourse.

sublevels.name: Literature of the Enlightenment
sublevels.description: The Literature of Enlightenment refers to the body of writing produced during the Enlightenment that championed reason, critical inquiry, and the questioning of traditional authority. It includes philosophical, political, and literary works that sought to promote individual freedom, scientific thinking, and social reform.

sublevels.name: Early Modern and Renaissance Literature
sublevels.description: Literature of the 16th, 17th and early 18th century.

sublevels.name: Shakespeare
sublevels.description: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor.

sublevels.name: Baroque
sublevels.description: Baroque is an artistic and cultural style that emerged in Europe during the 17th century, flourishing until the mid-18th century. It is characterized by grandeur, ornate details, dramatic expression, and a sense of movement. The Baroque style is found in various art forms, including architecture, painting, sculpture, music, literature, and theater.

sublevels.name: Seventeenth-Century Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works written in the seventeenth century, between 1600 and 1699. Literature from this period is characterized by a questioning attitude to matters of knowledge, faith and authority in religion, metaphysics, ethics, politics, economics and natural science.

sublevels.name: Nineteenth-Century Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works written between 1800 and 1899. Includes literary realism, Romantic literature and Victorian literature. May also cover literary works published over the course of the Long Nineteenth Century, from 1780 to 1919, especially fin de siecle writing.

sublevels.name: Romanticism
sublevels.description: Romanticism refers to a cultural and artistic movement that emerged in the late 18th century and flourished throughout the 19th century. It was a reaction against the rationality and restraint of the Enlightenment era and embraced emotion, individualism, imagination, and a fascination with nature and the past.

sublevels.name: Realism
sublevels.description: Realism, in the context of literature and art, refers to an artistic movement that emerged in the 19th century as a reaction against romanticism. Realism aims to depict the world as it is, presenting a truthful and objective representation of everyday life, social conditions, and human experiences. Realism in literature often focuses on ordinary people and their struggles, portraying their lives with attention to detail, accuracy, and psychological depth.

sublevels.name: Victorian Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works written during the reign of Queen Victoria, from 1837 to 1901. Poets and novelists during the Victorian era began to reflect on realities such as factory work, the plight of the lower class, and the treatment of women and children.

sublevels.name: Medieval Literature
sublevels.description: any work written in Latin or the vernacular between c. 476-1500 CE, including philosophy, religious treatises, legal texts, as well as works of the imagination.

sublevels.name: Twentieth-Century Literature
sublevels.description: Literary works written in the twentieth century, from 1900 to 1999. Includes major literary movements such as modernism and postmodernism, as well as Edwardian literature and writing of the First World War, Second World War and Cold War.

sublevels.name: Modernism
sublevels.description: Modernism refers to a cultural and intellectual movement that emerged in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is characterized by a break from traditional forms and conventions, embracing innovation, experimentation, and a critical examination of established norms and beliefs. Modernism can be observed in various fields such as art, literature, architecture, music, and philosophy.

sublevels.name: Postmodern Literature
sublevels.description: Postmodern literature refers to a literary movement that emerged in the mid-20th century as a response and departure from the principles of modernism. It is characterized by a playful, self-reflexive, and fragmented narrative style that often challenges traditional notions of authorship, meaning, and reality. Postmodern literature often incorporates elements of intertextuality, metafiction, irony, and cultural references.

sublevels.name: Literary Region or Country
sublevels.description: In literature regionalism refers to fiction or poetry that focuses on specific features, such as dialect, customs, history, and landscape, of a particular region (also called "local colour"). The setting is particularly important in regional literature and the "locale is likely to be rural and/or provincial.

sublevels.name: Latin American/Caribbean Literature
sublevels.description: Literature from Latin America (South America) and the Caribbean, both oral and written. Includes both literary works written in Spanish, Portuguese, indigenous languages of the Americas, French, English and Dutch.

sublevels.name: European Literature
sublevels.description: Literature from Europe, encompassing both Western and Eastern European literary traditions. Includes literary works written in European languages and works in translation.

sublevels.name: Scandinavian Literature
sublevels.description: Scandinavian literature refers to the literary works produced in the countries of Scandinavia, which include Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland (including Finnish-speaking areas), and Iceland. Scandinavian literature encompasses a rich literary tradition spanning various genres, themes, and time periods.

sublevels.name: Romanic Literature
sublevels.description: Romantic literature is marked by six primary characteristics: celebration of nature, focus on the individual and spirituality, celebration of isolation and melancholy, interest in the common man, idealization of women, and personification and pathetic fallacy.

sublevels.name: Slavic Literature
sublevels.description: Slavic literature refers to the literary works produced by Slavic-speaking peoples, who primarily reside in Central, Eastern, and Southeastern Europe. Slavic literature encompasses a diverse range of languages, including Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, Bulgarian, Serbian, Croatian, Slovenian, and others.

sublevels.name: British and Irish Literature
sublevels.description: Literature originating from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, the Isle of Man, the Channel Islands and Ireland.

sublevels.name: German Literature
sublevels.description: German literature refers to the body of literary works written in the German language or by German-speaking authors. It encompasses a rich and diverse tradition that spans many centuries and includes various genres and styles. German literature has made significant contributions to world literature, with renowned authors and works that have had a profound impact on literary movements and cultural discourse.

sublevels.name: Baltic Literature
sublevels.description: Baltic literature refers to the body of literature produced in the Baltic states, which include Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Baltic literature encompasses works written in the native languages of these countries, namely Estonian, Latvian, and Lithuanian, as well as literature produced by Baltic authors in other languages. Baltic literature holds a rich and diverse cultural heritage, often shaped by historical, social, and political contexts.

sublevels.name: Middle Eastern Literature
sublevels.description: Literature from the Middle East, either oral or written. Includes literary works written in Arabic, Hebrew, Persian, Turkish, Kurdish, and other Middle Eastern languages, as well as Anglophone works by authors from the Middle East and works in translation.

sublevels.name: Australasian Literature
sublevels.description: Australasian Literature encompasses the literary works produced in Australia, New Zealand, and the Pacific Islands, reflecting the region's diverse cultures, histories, and contemporary issues.

sublevels.name: African Literature
sublevels.description: Literature from Africa, either oral or written. Includes both literary works written in African and Afro-Asiatic languages, as well as literature written in other languages (Anglophone, Francophone) by African writers and works in translation.

sublevels.name: Asian Literature
sublevels.description: Asian Literature encompasses the literary works produced in Asia, reflecting the diverse cultures, histories, and languages of the continent, and includes both classical and contemporary texts.

sublevels.name: North American Literature
sublevels.description: Literature from the United States of America and Canada, including African American literature, Hispanic American literature, indigenous literatures and North American disaporic literatures.

sublevels.name: World Literature
sublevels.description: World literature is used to refer to the total of the world's national literature and the circulation of works into the wider world beyond their country of origin.

sublevels.name: Literature and Technology
sublevels.description: Literature and technology are two interconnected fields that have influenced and impacted each other throughout history. Literature often reflects the influence of technology on society, exploring its impact on individuals, relationships, and the human experience. Science fiction is a literary genre that often explores the implications of technology on society and imagines future advancements.

sublevels.name: Net Literature
sublevels.description: Net literature, also known as digital literature or electronic literature, refers to literary works created specifically for digital platforms and the internet. It encompasses literary works that are designed to be experienced through digital media and take advantage of the interactive, multimedia, and hypertextual capabilities offered by digital technologies.

sublevels.name: Digital Humanities
sublevels.description: e-Humanities, Computing in the Humanities or Digital Humanities means the systematic use of digital resources in the humanities, as well as the analysis of their application.

sublevels.name: Literature Business
sublevels.description: The term "business literature" encompasses the broad range of written materials that companies use to market their goods and services. Examples of business literature include publications as disparate as product catalogs, service brochures, and corporate newsletters.

sublevels.name: Literary Genre
sublevels.description: A literary genre is a category or classification of literature characterized by specific themes, narrative structures, and stylistic features. Genres provide a way to categorize and organize works of literature based on shared characteristics and conventions

sublevels.name: Non-Fiction Literature
sublevels.description: Non-fiction (or nonfiction) is any document or media content that attempts, in good faith, to convey information only about the real world, rather than being grounded in imagination. Non-fiction typically aims to present topics objectively based on historical, scientific, and empirical information. However, some non-fiction ranges into more subjective territory, including sincerely held opinions on real-world topics.

sublevels.name: Children's Literature
sublevels.description: The genre encompasses a wide range of works, including acknowledged classics of world literature, picture books and easy-to-read stories written exclusively for children, and fairy tales, lullabies, fables, folk songs, and other primarily orally transmitted materials.

sublevels.name: Poetry and Poetics
sublevels.description: literary work in which special intensity is given to the expression of feelings and ideas by the use of distinctive style and rhythm; poems collectively or as a genre of literature.

sublevels.name: Fiction Literature
sublevels.description: Fiction literature is any creative work, chiefly any narrative work, portraying people, events, or places in ways that are imaginary, or not strictly based on history or fact

sublevels.name: Gothic Fiction
sublevels.description: Gothic fiction, sometimes called Gothic horror in the 20th century, is a loose literary aesthetic of fear and haunting.

sublevels.name: Science Fiction
sublevels.description: fiction based on imagined future scientific or technological advances and major social or environmental changes, frequently portraying space or time travel and life on other planets.

sublevels.name: Crime Fiction
sublevels.description: Crime fiction, detective story, murder mystery, mystery novel, and police novel are terms used to describe narratives that centre on criminal acts and especially on the investigation, either by an amateur or a professional detective, of a serious crime, generally a murder.

sublevels.name: Fantasy Fiction
sublevels.description: Fantasy is a genre of speculative fiction involving magical elements, typically set in a fictional universe and sometimes inspired by mythology and folklore.

sublevels.name: Narrative Text and Prose
sublevels.description: Prose is any piece of writing that's not poetry. Narrative prose is a story with a plot and characters, and a short story is basically the same thing. Narrative prose can have some poetic elements including figurative language or imagery, but it's not written using a metrical structure or rhyme.

sublevels.name: Novel
sublevels.description: a fictitious prose narrative of book length, typically representing character and action with some degree of realism.

sublevels.name: Life Writing
sublevels.description: This genre encompasses autobiography, biography and other accounts of personal experience and memory, such as memoir, diaries, letters, testimonies, personal essays and digital forms like blogs and email.

sublevels.name: Epic
sublevels.description: In literature, an epic is a genre of narrative poetry that typically tells a long and grandiose story of heroic deeds and adventures. Epics often focus on the actions of legendary or mythological heroes, exploring themes of courage, heroism, honor, and the struggle between good and evil.

sublevels.name: Short Story
sublevels.description: a story with a fully developed theme but significantly shorter and less elaborate than a novel.

sublevels.name: Drama
sublevels.description: Drama is a literary genre that encompasses plays, scripts, and theatrical works. It is characterized by its intended performance on stage, where actors bring the written text to life through their interpretations and actions. Drama often explores conflicts, emotions, and interpersonal relationships, providing a platform for human experiences and social commentary.

sublevels.name: Literary Theory
sublevels.description: the field of study concerned with the principles underlying the analysis and understanding of literary works

sublevels.name: Deconstruction
sublevels.description: Deconstruction doesn't actually mean "demolition;" instead it means "breaking down" or analyzing something (especially the words in a work of fiction or nonfiction) to discover its true significance, which is supposedly almost never exactly what the author intended.

sublevels.name: Comparative Literature
sublevels.description: Comparative Literature is traditionally known as the study of two or more literatures in comparison (English and German, for example) and their multi-dimensional components which may encompass aspects such as the historical, gender, economic, cultural, social, philosophical, religious, and linguistic factors of the distinct cultures being analyzed.

sublevels.name: Literature and Cultural Studies
sublevels.description: Literature and cultural studies are interconnected fields that examine and analyze the relationship between literature and culture. While literature focuses on the study of written works, cultural studies explore broader cultural phenomena and social practices. Literature studies involve the analysis and interpretation of literary texts, including novels, poetry, plays, and essays. Cultural studies analyze and interpret cultural artifacts, practices, and phenomena, such as art, media, film, music, fashion, and popular culture.

sublevels.name: Translation Studies
sublevels.description: Translation studies is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the theory, practice, and analysis of translation and interpreting. It involves the examination of various aspects of translation, including the process, strategies, cultural considerations, and the impact of translation on language and communication.

sublevels.name: Literary Aesthetics
sublevels.description: Aesthetics, in literature, is the inclusion of references to artistic elements or expressions within a textual work. It's a method used to promote or educate readers about important artistic expression in society.

sublevels.name: Feminist Literary Theory
sublevels.description: Modern feminist literary theory seeks to understand both the literary portrayals and representation of both women and people in the queer community, expanding the role of a variety of identities and analysis within feminist literary criticism.

sublevels.name: Narratology
sublevels.description: Narratology is the study of narrative and narrative structure and the ways that these affect human perception.

sublevels.name: Ecocriticism
sublevels.description: Ecocriticism is the study of literature and ecology from an interdisciplinary point of view, where literature scholars analyze texts that illustrate environmental concerns and examine the various ways literature treats the subject of nature.

sublevels.name: Intermediality
sublevels.description: Intermediality, in other words, is not only the general term that defines the relationships between autonomous media, it is also the term that identifies the internal plurality of each medium. The intermedial study of literature therefore does not only refer to the study of the relationships between the literary text and its “others” (for instance the illustrations that accompany it, to give an elementary example), it also includes the study of the literary as a heterogeneous material that conveys a more or less radical “semiotic rupture” within itself (for instance when we interpret aspects of typography, from typeface to page layout and book design, as aspects of the text’s visuality—a dimension of literature that has always been at the center of visual and experimental poetry).

sublevels.name: Literary Methods
sublevels.description: Literary Methods refer to the various approaches and techniques used in the analysis and interpretation of literary texts, including close reading, structuralism, and postcolonial criticism.

sublevels.name: Literature and Pedagogy
sublevels.description: A pedagogical literature review is a synthesis of what has been published by scholars and researchers on some aspect of teaching and learning.

sublevels.name: Stylistics
sublevels.description: Stylistics is a branch of linguistics and literary analysis that focuses on the study of style in language and literature. It explores how linguistic choices, such as vocabulary, syntax, and figurative language, contribute to the overall meaning and impact of a text. Stylistics examines the way language is used to convey meaning beyond the literal level.

sublevels.name: Literary Diction
sublevels.description: Diction is a writer's or speaker's distinctive vocabulary choices and style of expression in a literary work, poem or story. In its common meaning, it is the distinctiveness of speech.

sublevels.name: Literary Interpretation
sublevels.description: Literary Interpretation is to find the meaning and significance of the story.

sublevels.name: Edition Science
sublevels.description: Edition Science deals with the practice, evolution, and future of scientific publishing. It explores topics such as peer review, open access, editorial processes, and the impact of digital technologies on research communication.

sublevels.name: Creative Writing
sublevels.description: Writing, typically fiction or poetry, which displays imagination or invention (in contrast to academic or journalistic writing). Characterized by an emphasis on narrative craft, character development, the use of literary tropes and various traditions of poetry and poetics.

sublevels.name: Rhetorics
sublevels.description: Rhetorics is the study of effective or persuasive speaking or writing, especially the use of figures of speech and other compositional techniques.

sublevels.name: Literary Criticism
sublevels.description: Literary criticism is the study, evaluation, and interpretation of literature.

sublevels.name: Literary Didactics
sublevels.description: The teaching of literature, especially focusing on the close reading of literary texts and how to write about literature. How literature is taught and examined, student responses to texts, resources for lecturers and supervisors.

sublevels.name: Media and Communication
sublevels.description: Media and communication are closely interconnected fields that involve the creation, transmission, and exchange of information, ideas, and messages. some key aspects of media and communication: Mass Media, Journalism, Digital Media, Advertising and Marketing, Public Relations

sublevels.name: Media Industries
sublevels.description: Media industries can be defined as a varied collection of organisations that share the production, publication and distribution of media. Industries include but are not limited to: news, publishing, film, music, social media, advertising, radio, games, TV, comics, books.

sublevels.name: Entertainment Industry
sublevels.description: The entertainment industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the various sectors involved in the creation, production, and distribution of entertainment products and services. This includes film, television, music, theater, sports, gaming, and digital media. The research within this field aims to understand the unique challenges and opportunities within each sector, including the impact of changing technologies, evolving consumer behaviors, and shifting market trends. Key topics within the entertainment industry as a field of research include audience engagement, content creation and distribution, intellectual property rights, marketing and advertising, and revenue generation.

sublevels.name: Printing and Publishing
sublevels.description: Research on the industry of making information, literature, music, software and other content available to the public for sale or for free. Traditionally, the term 'publishing' refers to the creation and distribution of printed works, such as books, newspapers, and magazines. With the advent of digital information systems, the scope has expanded to include electronic publishing such as ebooks, academic journals, micropublishing, websites, blogs, video game publishing, and the like.

sublevels.name: Radio
sublevels.description: Radio studies explores radio culture and the radio industry, the meaning of radio, both for the individual listener and for its place in wider society. Includes the study of acoustics, public service broadcasting, DJs, radio dramas, phone-ins, talk radio, radio advertising, internet and digital radio, news and much more.

sublevels.name: Science Communication
sublevels.description: The practice of informing, educating, raising awareness of science-related topics, and increasing the sense of wonder about scientific discoveries and arguments. Science communicators and audiences are ambiguously defined and the expertise and level of science knowledge varies with each group. Two types of science communication are outward-facing or science outreach (typically conducted by professional scientists to non-expert audiences) and inward-facing or science "inreach" (expert to expert communication from similar or different scientific backgrounds). Examples of outreach include science journalism and science museums. Examples of inreach include scholarly communication and publication in scientific journals.

sublevels.name: Library Science
sublevels.description: Library science (often termed library studies, bibliothecography, and library economy) is an interdisciplinary or multidisciplinary field that applies the practices, perspectives, and tools of management, information technology, education, and other areas to libraries; the collection, organization, preservation, and dissemination of information resources; and the political economy of information.

sublevels.name: Public Engagement with Science
sublevels.description: Public engagement with science describes intentional, meaningful interactions that provide opportunities for mutual learning between scientists and members of the public.

sublevels.name: Rhetoric of Science and Technology
sublevels.description: Rhetorical inquiry is a multidisciplinary field of study devoted to the critical examination of discourse. Initiated in classical times, it cultivates an "ability, in each [particular] case, to see the available means of persuasion". As an academic field, rhetoric of science and technology is the study of how scientists and non-scientists use arguments to advance claims about science and technology.

sublevels.name: Environmental Communication
sublevels.description: The dissemination of information and implementation of communication practices related to the environment. A broad field that includes research and practices regarding how different institutions, states, and people interact with regard to topics related to the environment and how cultural products influence society toward environmental issues.

sublevels.name: Technological Discourse
sublevels.description: Analysis of the impacts of industrial and digital technologies.

sublevels.name: Health Communication
sublevels.description: The study and practice of communicating promotional health information, such as in public health campaigns, health education, and between doctor and patient. The purpose of disseminating health information is to influence personal health choices by improving health literacy. Health communication is a unique niche in healthcare that allows professionals to use communication strategies to inform and influence decisions and actions of the public to improve health.

sublevels.name: Public Understanding of Science
sublevels.description: Relates to the attitudes, behaviours, opinions, and activities that comprise the relations between the general public or lay society as a whole to scientific knowledge and organisations.

sublevels.name: Journalism
sublevels.description: Journalism is the production and distribution of reports on the interaction of events, facts, ideas, and people that are the "news of the day" and that informs society to at least some degree. The word applies to the occupation (professional or not), the methods of gathering information, and the organizing literary styles. Journalistic media include: print, television, radio, Internet, and, in the past, newsreels.

sublevels.name: Audio Journalism
sublevels.description: The production and distribution of reports on the interaction of events, facts, ideas, and people to inform society, via audio methods such as radio and podcasts.

sublevels.name: Multimedia Journalism
sublevels.description: Multimedia journalism is the practice of contemporary journalism that distributes news content either using two or more media formats via the Internet, or disseminating news report via multiple media platforms. It is inseparably related to the media convergence of communication technologies, business integration of news industries, and editorial strategies of newsroom management.

sublevels.name: News Journalism
sublevels.description: News is information about current events. This may be provided through many different media: word of mouth, printing, postal systems, broadcasting, electronic communication, or through the testimony of observers and witnesses to events.

sublevels.name: Writing and Reporting
sublevels.description: A report is a document that presents information in an organized format for a specific audience and purpose. Although summaries of reports may be delivered orally, complete reports are almost always in the form of written documents

sublevels.name: Visual Journalism
sublevels.description: Visual journalism is the practice of strategically combining words and images to convey information.

sublevels.name: Film and Television Studies
sublevels.description: Film studies is an academic discipline that deals with various theoretical, historical, and critical approaches to cinema as an art form and a medium. Television studies is an academic discipline that deals with critical approaches to television.

sublevels.name: Australasian Film and TV
sublevels.description: The study of film and television from Australia and New Zealand

sublevels.name: Latin American Film and TV
sublevels.description: The study of the historical and cultural contexts of film and television practices in Latin America, as well as Latin American film and television texts themselves.

sublevels.name: Audio-Visual Culture
sublevels.description: Audio-visual culture means the practices, technologies, and social meanings through which societies produce, circulate, and interpret combined sound‑and‑image media.

sublevels.name: Screen Music and Sound
sublevels.description: Screen Music and Sound means the composition of sound and music for screen-based media like TV, film, and video games.

sublevels.name: Animation
sublevels.description: Animation is a process of creating the illusion of movement through the rapid display of a sequence of static images. It involves the use of various techniques, such as drawings, computer-generated imagery (CGI), stop motion, or a combination of these methods, to bring characters, objects, and scenes to life.

sublevels.name: Film Theory
sublevels.description: Film theory encompasses various approaches and frameworks for analyzing and interpreting films as artistic and cultural texts. It involves the study of the formal elements of cinema, the historical and social contexts of film production and reception, and the theoretical frameworks used to understand the medium. some key aspects and concepts related to film theory Auteur Theory, Formalism, Genre Theory, Semiotics.

sublevels.name: Screenwriting
sublevels.description: The study of screenwriting and scriptwriting

sublevels.name: Film and Television Production
sublevels.description: Film and television production refers to the process of creating audiovisual content for film and television. It involves various stages and activities to bring a project to life, from script development and pre-production to filming, post-production, and distribution.

sublevels.name: Global Film and TV
sublevels.description: Global film and TV refer to the production, distribution, and consumption of films and television shows on an international scale. It encompasses the global nature of the entertainment industry, where content is created in one country and distributed and consumed by audiences worldwide.

sublevels.name: Asian Film and TV
sublevels.description: Studies of film and television from Asian continent

sublevels.name: Experimental Film
sublevels.description: The study of experimental cinema, art film or artists' moving image

sublevels.name: Television Studies
sublevels.description: The study of television

sublevels.name: British Film and TV
sublevels.description: British film and TV refer to the productions and industries based in the United Kingdom that encompass filmmaking, television series, and other audiovisual content.

sublevels.name: Film and Television Industry
sublevels.description: The film and television industry refers to the collection of businesses involved in the creation, production, distribution, and exhibition of films and television shows. It is a multifaceted industry that encompasses various aspects, including: Film Production, Distribution and Exhibition, Broadcasting, Streaming Platforms.  It brings together professionals such as filmmakers, producers, directors, writers, actors, technicians, and many others who contribute to the creation of captivating visual storytelling experiences enjoyed by audiences worldwide.

sublevels.name: Close Readings in Film and TV
sublevels.description: Study of film and television characterised by close textual analysis

sublevels.name: Directing
sublevels.description: The study of directing and directors for film and television

sublevels.name: Documentary Studies
sublevels.description: The study of documentaries

sublevels.name: European Film and TV
sublevels.description: The study of film and television from the European continent

sublevels.name: Adaptation Studies
sublevels.description: A pre-existing work that has been made into a film. Adaptations are often of literary or theatrical works, but musical theatre, best-selling fiction and non-fiction, comic books, computer games, children's toys, and so on have also been regularly adapted for the cinema.

sublevels.name: Genre Studies
sublevels.description: The study of genre in film and television including Horror OR Science Fiction OR Comedy OR Thriller OR Musical OR Film Noir Or Fantasy OR Action Adventure

sublevels.name: American Film and TV
sublevels.description: The study of film and television from USA

sublevels.name: Screen Performance
sublevels.description: Screen performance refers to the act of portraying a character or delivering a performance specifically intended for the screen, whether in film, television, or other forms of visual media. It involves the interpretation and portrayal of characters through acting techniques tailored for the camera.

sublevels.name: Film and TV History
sublevels.description: The study of the history of film and television

sublevels.name: African Film and TV
sublevels.description: Film and television studies from African continent.

sublevels.name: Media Law
sublevels.description: The legislation through which governments regulate the mass media. It includes issues of censorship, copyright, defamation, broadcast law, and antitrust law. In democracies, media law is seen as a balancing act between two conflicting principles: freedom of expression and constraints laid down in statutes of common law, as in issues of defamation and the national interest.

sublevels.name: Media Ethics
sublevels.description: Media ethics is a division of applied ethics dealing with the specific ethical principles and standards of media, including broadcast media, film, theatre, the arts, print media and the internet.

sublevels.name: Media and Communication Theory
sublevels.description: Media and communication theories are explanations and predictions of social phenomena that attempt to relate media and communication to various aspects of our personal and cultural lives or social systems.

sublevels.name: Media and Communication Methods
sublevels.description: A field covering research methods and techniques, including research design, the collection, analysis and interpretation of data in media and communication studies.

sublevels.name: Media Reception and Media Effects
sublevels.description: Media influence and media effects are topics relating to mass media and media culture's effects on individual or an audience's thoughts, attitudes, and behavior. Whether it is written, televised, or spoken, mass media reaches a large audience. Mass media's role and effect in shaping modern culture are central issues for study of culture.

sublevels.name: Children, Youth and Media
sublevels.description: Multidisciplinary perspectives on a wide range of research topics, addressing children and youth from infancy to young adulthood, whether framed in terms of child and adolescent psychosocial development, critical constructions of ‘youth’, cultural analyses of childhood in diverse settings, media effects or media design issues.

sublevels.name: Media Economics
sublevels.description: Economic aspects of the media system, especially from a communication science perspective: media economics is thus not limited to the consideration of economic aspects of the media system, but also considers the consequences of economization for the entire communication and information system of a society

sublevels.name: Media Policy and Politics
sublevels.description: Media policy and politics refer to the interactions and relationships between the media industry, governmental bodies, and political institutions. It involves the development, implementation, and regulation of policies and laws that shape the media landscape and influence the role of media in society.

sublevels.name: Development Communication
sublevels.description: Development Communication refers to the use of communication to facilitate social development. Development communication techniques include information dissemination and education, behaviour change, social marketing, social mobilization, media advocacy, communication for social change and community participation.

sublevels.name: Political Communication
sublevels.description: Political communication is concerned with the creation, content, exchange, spread and effect of information between the citizenry and the political entities, policy makers, government officials, and other related set-ups, via different kinds of media, and throughout all stages of the political process.

sublevels.name: Cyber Politics
sublevels.description: How politicians and political parties use the internet/online spaces for various activities including election campaigns, keeping in touch with constituents, and forging alliances with other groups or individuals. The internet may also enable small groups with limited resources to participate in the political process.

sublevels.name: Media and Communication History
sublevels.description: Media and communication history refers to the study and exploration of the development and evolution of various forms of media and communication throughout human history. It involves examining the technologies, practices, institutions, and social implications of media and communication over time. Studying media and communication history provides insights into the social, cultural, and technological forces that have shaped human communication practices and the role of media in society. It allows for an understanding of how media and communication have evolved, influenced culture and politics, and shaped our contemporary media landscape.

sublevels.name: Digital and New Media
sublevels.description: An academic discipline that explores the intersections of computing, science, the humanities, and the visual and performing arts. The main factor in defining new media is the role the Internet plays; new media is effortlessly spread instantly. The category of new media is occupied by devices connected to the Internet, an example being a smartphone or tablet.

sublevels.name: Media Design
sublevels.description: A mixed discipline between design and information-development which is concerned with how media communicate with people.

sublevels.name: Digital Journalism
sublevels.description: Digital journalism, also known as online journalism, is a contemporary form of journalism where editorial content is distributed via the Internet, as opposed to publishing via print or broadcast.

sublevels.name: Social Media
sublevels.description: Forms of electronic communication (such as websites for social networking and microblogging) through which users create online communities to share information, ideas, personal messages, and other content.  Social Media studies explores the relationship to and impact of this form of communication on culture, society, psychology, politics etc.

sublevels.name: Internet Studies
sublevels.description: Internet studies is an interdisciplinary field studying the social, psychological, pedagogical, political, technical, cultural, artistic, and other dimensions of the Internet and associated information and communication technologies.

sublevels.name: Organizational and Strategic Communication
sublevels.description: Strategic communication can mean either communicating a concept, a process, or data that satisfies a long-term strategic goal of an organization by allowing facilitation of advanced planning, or communicating over long distances usually using international telecommunications or dedicated global network assets to coordinate actions and activities of operationally significant commercial, non-commercial and military business or combat and logistic subunits. It can also mean the related function within an organization, which handles internal and external communication processes. Strategic communication can also be used for political warfare.

sublevels.name: Advertising
sublevels.description: The activity or profession of producing advertisements for commercial products or services.

sublevels.name: Public Relations
sublevels.description: Public relations (PR) is the practice of managing and disseminating information from an individual or an organization (such as a business, government agency, or a nonprofit organization) to the public in order to affect their public perception. Public relations (PR) and publicity differ in that PR is controlled internally, whereas publicity is not controlled and contributed by external parties.

sublevels.name: Corporate Communication
sublevels.description: Corporate communication research is a subfield of business and management research that examines how organizations communicate with their various stakeholders, including employees, customers, investors, and the general public. It involves the study of communication strategies and practices that organizations use to achieve their goals, as well as the effects of these communication activities on the attitudes and behaviors of stakeholders. The research topics within corporate communication research may include: Analysis of communication channels used by organizations to reach their stakeholders Evaluation of the effectiveness of different communication strategies and practices Examination of the impact of organizational communication on stakeholders' attitudes and behaviors Investigation of the role of communication in organizational change and crisis management Study of the relationship between corporate communication and organizational reputation and image Analysis of the ethical dimensions of organizational communication Corporate communication research can inform business and management practices by providing insights into effective communication strategies that can help organizations achieve their goals and maintain positive relationships with their stakeholders. Additionally, research in this area can inform public policy and regulatory efforts aimed at promoting ethical and effective corporate communication practices.

sublevels.name: Communication of Non-Profit Organizations
sublevels.description: Nonprofit communications encompasses a wide range of tools that organizations can use to get their message across.

sublevels.name: Media Culture
sublevels.description: Media culture refers to the current Western capitalist society that emerged and developed from the 20th century, under the influence of mass media. The term alludes to the overall impact and intellectual guidance exerted by the media (primarily TV, but also the press, radio and cinema), not only on public opinion but also on tastes and values.

sublevels.name: Comics Studies
sublevels.description: Comics studies is an academic field that focuses on comics & graphic novels, and sequential art.

sublevels.name: Games Studies
sublevels.description: Games studies is an interdisciplinary field of academic study that focuses on the analysis, interpretation, and understanding of games and gaming culture.
